definition: The occurrence of fortunate events by happy accident.
etymology: Coined in 1754 by Horace Walpole from the Persian fairy tale 'The Three Princes of Serendip,' whose heroes were always making lucky discoveries.
exampleSentence: Finding that old bookstore on a rainy afternoon was pure serendipity.

definition: The pleasant earthy smell that rises from dry soil after rain.
etymology: Coined in 1964 by Australian researchers Bear and Thomas from Greek 'petra' (stone) and 'ichor' (the fluid in the veins of the gods).
exampleSentence: She opened the window just to breathe in the petrichor after the storm.

definition: Fluent and persuasive in speaking or writing.
etymology: From Latin 'eloqui,' meaning to speak out, combining 'e-' (out) and 'loqui' (to speak).
exampleSentence: His eloquent toast at the wedding made half the room cry.

definition: Able to recover quickly from difficulty or change.
etymology: From Latin 'resilire,' meaning to leap back or rebound.
exampleSentence: Kids are surprisingly resilient when their routines get shaken up.

definition: Sweet or musical; pleasant to hear.
etymology: From Late Latin 'mellifluus,' combining 'mel' (honey) and 'fluere' (to flow).
exampleSentence: The narrator had such a mellifluous voice I would have listened to him read the phone book.

definition: A sentimental longing for a period in the past.
etymology: Coined in 1688 by Swiss physician Johannes Hofer from Greek 'nostos' (homecoming) and 'algos' (pain) to describe a medical condition in soldiers.
exampleSentence: Hearing that song hit me with a wave of nostalgia for high school summers.

definition: Showing great attention to detail; very thorough.
etymology: From Latin 'meticulosus,' originally meaning fearful, from 'metus' (fear); the modern sense of carefulness developed in the 19th century.
exampleSentence: She's meticulous about her notebooks — every page is dated and color-coded.

definition: Fond of the company of others; sociable.
etymology: From Latin 'gregarius,' meaning belonging to a flock, from 'grex' (flock or herd).
exampleSentence: He's so gregarious he'll strike up a conversation with anyone in line.

definition: Pleasantly relaxed and unhurried; lacking energy.
etymology: From Latin 'languidus,' from 'languere' (to be weak or faint).
exampleSentence: They spent a languid Sunday on the porch, doing nothing in particular.

definition: A sudden, striking realization or insight.
etymology: From Greek 'epiphaneia,' meaning manifestation or appearance, originally referring to the showing of a deity.
exampleSentence: I had a tiny epiphany in the shower about why my code wasn't compiling.

definition: Present or found everywhere.
etymology: From Latin 'ubique,' meaning everywhere, formed from 'ubi' (where).
exampleSentence: Phone chargers have become so ubiquitous you forget how recent they are.

definition: Providing emotional release or cleansing.
etymology: From Greek 'katharsis,' meaning cleansing or purging, used by Aristotle to describe the effect of tragedy.
exampleSentence: A long, ugly cry can be weirdly cathartic.

definition: Dealing with things sensibly and realistically.
etymology: From Greek 'pragmatikos,' meaning fit for business, from 'pragma' (deed or affair).
exampleSentence: She took a pragmatic approach: fix what you can, ignore what you can't.

definition: Holding firmly; persistent and determined.
etymology: From Latin 'tenax,' meaning holding fast, from 'tenere' (to hold).
exampleSentence: He's tenacious about his sourdough starter — he's kept it alive for six years.

definition: Attractively lively and animated.
etymology: From Latin 'vivax,' meaning long-lived or lively, from 'vivere' (to live).
exampleSentence: Her vivacious laugh carried across the entire restaurant.

definition: Lasting for a very short time.
etymology: From Greek 'ephemeros,' meaning lasting only a day, from 'epi-' (on) and 'hemera' (day).
exampleSentence: Cherry blossoms are beautiful precisely because they're so ephemeral.

definition: Representing the most perfect example of something.
etymology: From medieval Latin 'quinta essentia,' the fifth element beyond earth, water, air, and fire that ancient philosophers believed permeated all things.
exampleSentence: That diner is the quintessential road trip stop — coffee, pie, and chrome stools.

definition: Proceeding in a gradual, subtle way with harmful effects.
etymology: From Latin 'insidiosus,' meaning cunning or deceitful, from 'insidiae' (ambush).
exampleSentence: Burnout is insidious — you don't notice it until you can't get out of bed.

definition: The realization that each passerby is living a life as vivid and complex as your own.
etymology: Coined in 2012 by John Koenig for his Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, borrowing the form of German 'sonder' (special) and French 'sonder' (to probe).
exampleSentence: Watching the crowd at the train station, I had a quiet moment of sonder.

definition: Having a vague, melancholy longing.
etymology: Formed in the 17th century, probably from earlier 'wistly' (intently), influenced by 'wishful.'
exampleSentence: He gave the old house a wistful glance as we drove away.

definition: Giving off light; radiant.
etymology: From Latin 'luminosus,' from 'lumen' (light).
exampleSentence: Her skin looked luminous in the candlelight.

definition: A feeling of intense happiness or excitement.
etymology: From Greek 'euphoria,' meaning the power of enduring easily, from 'eu-' (well) and 'pherein' (to bear).
exampleSentence: Finishing the marathon gave him a kind of euphoria that lasted for days.

definition: A pensive, gentle sadness.
etymology: From Greek 'melankholia,' meaning black bile, one of the four bodily humors that ancient medicine believed caused this mood.
exampleSentence: Autumn always brings a sweet melancholy with it.

definition: A strong desire to travel.
etymology: Borrowed from German in the early 1900s, literally 'desire to wander.'
exampleSentence: Two weeks at home and the wanderlust hits again.

definition: To walk in a slow, relaxed manner.
etymology: Origin obscure; recorded in the 17th century, possibly from Middle English 'santren' (to muse).
exampleSentence: He sauntered into the meeting twenty minutes late and didn't apologize.

definition: To think deeply about something for a long time.
etymology: From Latin 'ruminari,' meaning to chew the cud, like cattle.
exampleSentence: She tends to ruminate on small comments for days.

definition: Denoting a period of time in the past that was idyllically happy and peaceful.
etymology: From Greek 'halkyon,' a mythical bird (identified with the kingfisher) believed to calm the seas during its breeding period.
exampleSentence: They still talk about the halcyon days of the band before the lineup changed.

definition: A temporary stay somewhere.
etymology: From Old French 'sojorner,' from Late Latin 'subdiurnare' (to spend the day), from 'sub' (under) and 'diurnus' (of a day).
exampleSentence: After a brief sojourn in Lisbon, she moved on to Madrid.

definition: Green with grass or other vegetation.
etymology: From Old French 'verdoyant,' from Latin 'viridis' (green).
exampleSentence: After all that rain, the hills were impossibly verdant.

definition: Bubbly and full of energy; vivacious.
etymology: From Latin 'effervescere,' meaning to boil up, from 'ex-' (out) and 'fervere' (to boil).
exampleSentence: She had an effervescent personality that filled the room.

definition: Glowing with intense heat or passion.
etymology: From Latin 'incandescere,' meaning to glow with heat, from 'in-' (within) and 'candescere' (to become white).
exampleSentence: He was incandescent with rage when he saw the dent in his car.

definition: A whispering, murmuring, or rustling sound.
etymology: From Latin 'susurrus,' meaning a whisper or hum, imitative in origin.
exampleSentence: There was a soft susurrus of pages turning in the library.

definition: Completely clear and transparent.
etymology: From Latin 'limpidus,' meaning clear, possibly related to 'lympha' (clear water).
exampleSentence: She has the limpid prose of someone who edits ruthlessly.

definition: Excessively sweet or sentimental.
etymology: From medieval Latin 'saccharum' (sugar), ultimately from Sanskrit 'sarkara' (gravel, ground sugar).
exampleSentence: The movie's ending was a little too saccharine for my taste.

definition: To throw someone or something out of a window.
etymology: From Latin 'de-' (down or away from) and 'fenestra' (window); the word gained currency after the 1618 Defenestration of Prague.
exampleSentence: If my laptop crashes one more time I'm going to defenestrate it.

definition: A person who flatters powerful people to gain advantage.
etymology: From Greek 'sykophantes,' literally 'fig-shower,' an informer in ancient Athens, though the exact connection to figs is lost.
exampleSentence: The CEO's office was full of sycophants laughing too hard at his jokes.

definition: To deliberately make something unclear or confusing.
etymology: From Latin 'obfuscare,' meaning to darken, from 'ob-' (over) and 'fuscus' (dark).
exampleSentence: The legal language seemed designed to obfuscate rather than clarify.

definition: To place two things close together for contrasting effect.
etymology: From Latin 'juxta' (next to) and French 'poser' (to place), coined in the 19th century.
exampleSentence: The gallery juxtaposed Renaissance portraits with modern selfies.

definition: Tending to talk a great deal.
etymology: From Latin 'loquax,' from 'loqui' (to speak).
exampleSentence: My grandfather gets loquacious after exactly one glass of wine.

definition: Reserved or uncommunicative in speech; saying little.
etymology: From Latin 'taciturnus,' from 'tacitus' (silent), past participle of 'tacere' (to be silent).
exampleSentence: He's taciturn in meetings but apparently hilarious at parties.

definition: Using more words than necessary.
etymology: From Latin 'verbosus,' from 'verbum' (word).
exampleSentence: The instructions were so verbose I couldn't find the actual step.

definition: Using very few words; concise to the point of brevity.
etymology: From Greek 'Lakonikos,' relating to Laconia (Sparta), whose citizens were famous for their terse speech.
exampleSentence: His laconic 'we'll see' was his version of an enthusiastic yes.

definition: Concise and forcefully expressive.
etymology: From Old English 'pitha' (the soft inner tissue of a plant), the figurative sense of 'substance' developing in the 16th century.
exampleSentence: She has a pithy comeback for every situation.

definition: Friendly, lively, and enjoyable.
etymology: From Latin 'convivium' (a feast), from 'con-' (together) and 'vivere' (to live).
exampleSentence: The dinner had a wonderfully convivial atmosphere.

definition: Mutual trust and friendship among people who spend time together.
etymology: From French 'camaraderie,' from 'camarade' (comrade), originally a Spanish soldier's term for someone you share a room with.
exampleSentence: There's a real camaraderie among the night shift.

definition: Evoking a keen sense of sadness or regret.
etymology: From Old French 'poignant,' present participle of 'poindre' (to prick), from Latin 'pungere'.
exampleSentence: The eulogy was simple and poignant.

definition: Of such excellence or beauty as to inspire awe.
etymology: From Latin 'sublimis,' meaning lofty or exalted, perhaps from 'sub-' (up to) and 'limen' (threshold).
exampleSentence: That first bite of fresh bread is sublime.

definition: A state of being pleasantly lost in one's thoughts; a daydream.
etymology: From Old French 'reverie,' meaning wild conduct or delirium, from 'rever' (to dream).
exampleSentence: I was deep in a reverie when the doorbell snapped me back.

definition: Shining brilliantly; radiant.
etymology: From Latin 'effulgere,' meaning to shine out, from 'ex-' (out) and 'fulgere' (to shine).
exampleSentence: She walked in looking absolutely effulgent in that red dress.

definition: Having a ready insight into and understanding of things.
etymology: From Latin 'perspicax,' meaning sharp-sighted, from 'perspicere' (to see through).
exampleSentence: Her perspicacious questions made everyone rethink the plan.

definition: Having keen mental discernment; wise.
etymology: From Latin 'sagax,' meaning of quick perception, related to 'sagire' (to perceive keenly).
exampleSentence: He's a sagacious investor — patient and very hard to fool.

definition: Having or showing great knowledge or learning.
etymology: From Latin 'eruditus,' meaning instructed or polished, from 'e-' (out) and 'rudis' (rough or untrained).
exampleSentence: Her essays are erudite but never dry.

definition: Excessively concerned with minor details or rules.
etymology: From Italian 'pedante,' a schoolmaster, possibly from Greek 'paideuein' (to teach).
exampleSentence: I don't mean to be pedantic, but technically that's a different species.

definition: Intended to teach, especially in a moralizing way.
etymology: From Greek 'didaktikos,' meaning skilled in teaching, from 'didaskein' (to teach).
exampleSentence: The novel got a bit didactic in the final chapters.

definition: Intended for or understood by only a small number of people.
etymology: From Greek 'esoterikos,' meaning belonging to the inner circle, from 'eso' (within).
exampleSentence: His hobbies are pretty esoteric — beekeeping and Latvian folk music.

definition: Understood by few; mysterious or secret.
etymology: From Latin 'arcanus,' meaning hidden or closed, from 'arca' (chest or box).
exampleSentence: Tax law is full of arcane rules nobody can really keep straight.

definition: So lacking in originality as to be obvious and boring.
etymology: From French 'banal,' originally meaning belonging to the feudal lord's domain and therefore commonplace.
exampleSentence: The small talk at the office party was painfully banal.

definition: Overused and lacking original thought.
etymology: From Latin 'tritus,' worn out, past participle of 'terere' (to rub).
exampleSentence: It sounds trite, but you really do have to be your own biggest fan.

definition: Very great or intense; showing deep insight.
etymology: From Latin 'profundus,' meaning deep, from 'pro-' (forward) and 'fundus' (bottom).
exampleSentence: Losing him had a profound effect on the whole family.

definition: The ability to make good judgments and quick decisions.
etymology: From Latin 'acumen,' meaning a point or sharpness, from 'acuere' (to sharpen).
exampleSentence: Her business acumen turned a side hustle into a real company.

definition: Brisk and cheerful readiness.
etymology: From Latin 'alacritas,' from 'alacer' (lively or eager).
exampleSentence: He accepted the invitation with alacrity.

definition: Self-confidence or assurance, especially in difficult situations.
etymology: From French 'aplomb,' literally 'according to the plumb line,' meaning upright or balanced.
exampleSentence: She handled the heckler with surprising aplomb.

definition: Flamboyant confidence of style or manner.
etymology: From French 'panache,' meaning a plume of feathers on a helmet, ultimately from Latin 'pinnaculum' (small wing).
exampleSentence: He cooks with real panache — there's always a flourish.

definition: Intricate and refined delicacy; tactful skill.
etymology: From French 'finesse,' from 'fin' (fine or refined).
exampleSentence: It takes finesse to break bad news without crushing someone.

definition: A learned person; someone with exceptional ability in a specific field.
etymology: From French 'savant,' present participle of 'savoir' (to know), from Latin 'sapere'.
exampleSentence: He's a coding savant who still can't operate a microwave.

definition: A person who speaks several languages.
etymology: From Greek 'polyglottos,' from 'poly-' (many) and 'glotta' (tongue).
exampleSentence: Working at the hostel turned her into a casual polyglot.

definition: A person who tells anecdotes in a skillful and amusing way.
etymology: From French 'raconter' (to recount), from 'conter' (to tell).
exampleSentence: My uncle is a born raconteur — every dinner is a one-man show.

definition: Cheerful friendliness; geniality.
etymology: From French 'bonhomie,' from 'bonhomme' (good-natured man).
exampleSentence: There's a relaxed bonhomie at the corner pub on Thursdays.

definition: Exuberant enjoyment of life.
etymology: Borrowed directly from French, literally 'joy of living,' popularized in English in the late 19th century.
exampleSentence: You can't be around her without catching a little of her joie de vivre.

definition: A feeling of listless dissatisfaction arising from lack of occupation or excitement.
etymology: From French 'ennui,' from Old French 'enui' (annoyance), ultimately from Latin 'in odio' (in hatred).
exampleSentence: Sunday afternoon ennui can be its own kind of suffering.

definition: A general feeling of discomfort or unease.
etymology: From Old French 'malaise,' literally 'bad ease,' from 'mal' (bad) and 'aise' (ease).
exampleSentence: There was a quiet malaise hanging over the whole department.

definition: A deep anxiety or dread, often about the human condition.
etymology: Borrowed from German and Danish 'angst,' from Old High German 'angust' (fear); popularized through Kierkegaard's philosophy.
exampleSentence: Teenage angst is universal but also strangely specific each time.

definition: Pleasure derived from another person's misfortune.
etymology: Borrowed from German, from 'Schaden' (damage) and 'Freude' (joy).
exampleSentence: I'll admit a tiny bit of schadenfreude when his perfect lawn got chickenpox.

definition: The defining spirit or mood of a particular period.
etymology: Borrowed from German, literally 'time-spirit,' popularized through Hegel.
exampleSentence: That show captured the zeitgeist of the early 2010s perfectly.

definition: A person who looks uncannily like someone else.
etymology: Borrowed from German 'Doppelgänger,' meaning 'double-goer,' originally a ghostly counterpart in folklore.
exampleSentence: My barista has a doppelganger on the morning train.

definition: A child prodigy; a person who achieves great success while young.
etymology: Borrowed from German 'Wunderkind,' meaning 'wonder-child.'
exampleSentence: He was a chess wunderkind who later became an unremarkable lawyer.

definition: Art or design considered to be in poor taste because of excessive sentimentality.
etymology: Borrowed from German 'Kitsch,' originally Munich art dealer slang of the 1860s for cheap art.
exampleSentence: Her apartment is gloriously full of kitsch — flamingos, lava lamps, and all.

definition: Composure or coolness shown in danger or under trying circumstances.
etymology: From French 'sang-froid,' literally 'cold blood.'
exampleSentence: He landed the plane with the sangfroid of someone parallel parking.

definition: Casual lack of concern; nonchalance.
etymology: From French 'insouciance,' from 'in-' (not) and 'soucier' (to trouble).
exampleSentence: He shrugged off the bad review with practiced insouciance.

definition: Feeling or appearing casually calm and relaxed.
etymology: From Old French 'nonchaloir,' meaning to disregard, from 'non-' (not) and 'chaloir' (to be concerned).
exampleSentence: She acted nonchalant about the promotion, but she was glowing.

definition: Confident, stylish, and charming.
etymology: From Old French 'de bon aire,' literally 'of good disposition.'
exampleSentence: He showed up in a linen suit looking absolutely debonair.

definition: Charming, confident, and elegant.
etymology: From Latin 'suavis,' meaning sweet or pleasant.
exampleSentence: The host was suave but the canapés were the real star.

definition: A confident, arrogant walk or manner.
etymology: Probably formed in the 16th century from 'swag' (to sway), of Scandinavian origin.
exampleSentence: He walked into the audition with a swagger that did not survive the first question.

definition: Enthusiastic and vigorous enjoyment.
etymology: From Italian 'gusto' (taste), from Latin 'gustus.'
exampleSentence: She attacks Sunday crosswords with gusto.

definition: Vigor and spirit, especially in artistic performance.
etymology: From French 'verve,' meaning vigor, originally a 16th-century word for a literary 'whim' or fancy.
exampleSentence: The band played the old standards with surprising verve.

definition: Great energy or enthusiasm for a cause or objective.
etymology: From Greek 'zelos,' meaning ardor or jealousy.
exampleSentence: His zeal for sourdough has taken over the kitchen counter.

definition: Intense and passionate feeling.
etymology: From Latin 'fervor,' meaning a boiling heat, from 'fervere' (to boil).
exampleSentence: There was a quiet fervor in the room as the votes were counted.

definition: Enthusiastic or passionate.
etymology: From Latin 'ardens,' present participle of 'ardere' (to burn).
exampleSentence: She's an ardent defender of the Oxford comma.

definition: Having a keen interest or enthusiasm.
etymology: From Latin 'avidus,' meaning eager or greedy, from 'avere' (to crave).
exampleSentence: He's an avid birder, binoculars permanently around his neck.

definition: Sharp; eager and enthusiastic.
etymology: From Old English 'cene,' meaning bold or wise, related to German 'kühn' (bold).
exampleSentence: She has a keen eye for vintage furniture.

definition: Having an ability to accurately assess situations and turn them to one's advantage.
etymology: From Latin 'astutus,' from 'astus' (craft or cunning).
exampleSentence: That was an astute question that nobody else thought to ask.

definition: Having sharp powers of judgment.
etymology: From Middle English 'shrewed' (depraved, malicious), past participle of 'shrewen' (to curse); the meaning shifted to clever in the 16th century.
exampleSentence: He's a shrewd negotiator — patient and willing to walk away.

definition: Having shrewdness and good judgment, especially in money matters.
etymology: From Scots 'canny,' from 'can' (to know how), of Germanic origin.
exampleSentence: My grandmother was canny with money in a way I'll never match.

definition: Acting with care and thought for the future.
etymology: From Latin 'prudens,' a contraction of 'providens' (foreseeing).
exampleSentence: It seemed prudent to leave before the snow got worse.

definition: Having or showing good judgment.
etymology: From Latin 'judicium' (judgment), from 'judex' (judge).
exampleSentence: A judicious use of butter improves almost any recipe.

definition: Having or showing good judgment, especially in matters of taste.
etymology: From Latin 'discernere,' meaning to separate or distinguish, from 'dis-' (apart) and 'cernere' (to sift).
exampleSentence: She has a discerning palate — she can tell you exactly which farm the cheese came from.

definition: Very attentive to accuracy and detail; hard to please.
etymology: From Latin 'fastidiosus,' meaning disdainful, from 'fastidium' (loathing).
exampleSentence: He's fastidious about his espresso — the grind has to be exactly right.

definition: Diligent, thorough, and extremely attentive to details.
etymology: From Latin 'scrupulus,' a small sharp stone (figuratively, a source of unease).
exampleSentence: She's scrupulous about citing her sources.

definition: Showing great attention to detail or correct behavior.
etymology: From Italian 'puntiglio,' meaning a fine point, from Latin 'punctum' (point).
exampleSentence: He's punctilious about thank-you notes in a way that's actually charming.

definition: Showing care and conscientiousness in one's work.
etymology: From Latin 'diligens,' meaning attentive, from 'diligere' (to value highly).
exampleSentence: He's a diligent student who actually reads the footnotes.

definition: Showing great care and perseverance.
etymology: From Latin 'assiduus,' meaning busy, from 'assidere' (to sit by).
exampleSentence: Her assiduous note-taking saved the whole project.

definition: Persisting tirelessly.
etymology: From Latin 'indefatigabilis,' from 'in-' (not) and 'defatigare' (to tire out).
exampleSentence: My mother is an indefatigable gardener — out there in any weather.

definition: Fearless; adventurous.
etymology: From Latin 'intrepidus,' from 'in-' (not) and 'trepidus' (alarmed).
exampleSentence: Our intrepid intern volunteered to fix the printer.

definition: Showing a willingness to take surprisingly bold risks.
etymology: From Latin 'audax,' from 'audere' (to dare).
exampleSentence: It was an audacious plan that probably shouldn't have worked, but did.

definition: Having or showing determined courage in difficulty.
etymology: From 'pluck' in the sense of guts or spirit, originally meaning the heart and viscera of an animal, considered the seat of courage.
exampleSentence: That plucky little dog tried to herd the geese.

definition: Showing courage or determination.
etymology: From Old French 'vaillant,' from Latin 'valere' (to be strong).
exampleSentence: A valiant effort at parallel parking, but the curb won.

definition: Enduring pain or hardship without showing feelings.
etymology: From Greek 'Stoa Poikile' (the Painted Porch in Athens), where the philosopher Zeno taught the doctrines that became Stoicism.
exampleSentence: He was stoic through the whole dental procedure, though I would have cried.

definition: Having an unemotional and stolidly calm disposition.
etymology: From Greek 'phlegmatikos,' relating to phlegm, one of the four bodily humors believed to cause a calm temperament.
exampleSentence: Our phlegmatic basset hound is unmoved by thunderstorms.

definition: Optimistic or cheerful, especially in a difficult situation.
etymology: From Latin 'sanguineus,' relating to blood, another of the four humors said to produce a cheerful temperament.
exampleSentence: She remained sanguine about her chances even after the second rejection.

definition: Easily angered; bad-tempered.
etymology: From Greek 'kholerikos,' from 'khole' (bile), one of the four humors associated with anger.
exampleSentence: He was a famously choleric coach who once threw a clipboard into the bleachers.

definition: Not easily upset or excited; calm.
etymology: From Latin 'placidus,' meaning pleasing or gentle, from 'placere' (to please).
exampleSentence: The lake was placid that morning, perfect for swimming.

definition: Calm, peaceful, and untroubled.
etymology: From Latin 'serenus,' meaning clear or unclouded (originally describing weather).
exampleSentence: There was something serene about her even on chaotic days.

definition: Free from disturbance; calm.
etymology: From Latin 'tranquillus,' meaning calm, possibly from 'trans-' (across) and 'quiescere' (to rest).
exampleSentence: They wanted a tranquil cabin somewhere with no Wi-Fi.

definition: Extremely happy, peaceful, or picturesque.
etymology: From Greek 'eidyllion,' meaning a short pastoral poem, a diminutive of 'eidos' (form).
exampleSentence: The little farm looked idyllic until I got close enough to smell the chickens.

definition: Relating to the pleasant aspects of the countryside.
etymology: From Greek 'boukolikos,' from 'boukolos' (cowherd), from 'bous' (cow).
exampleSentence: They left the city for a bucolic stretch of Vermont and never looked back.

definition: Of or relating to country life, especially in an idealized way.
etymology: From Latin 'pastoralis,' from 'pastor' (shepherd).
exampleSentence: The painting was a pastoral scene of sheep and rolling hills.

definition: Consisting of or associated with woods or forests.
etymology: From Latin 'silva' (wood or forest).
exampleSentence: There's a sylvan path behind the house that leads to a quiet creek.

definition: Living in or relating to trees.
etymology: From Latin 'arbor' (tree).
exampleSentence: Squirrels are surprisingly bold for such an arboreal species.

definition: Lush green vegetation.
etymology: From Old French 'verdure,' from 'verd' (green), from Latin 'viridis.'
exampleSentence: After the rains, the hills were thick with verdure.

definition: The leaves of a plant or trees.
etymology: From Old French 'fueillage,' from 'fueille' (leaf), from Latin 'folium.'
exampleSentence: The foliage in October makes the whole drive worth it.

definition: Relating to or active at twilight.
etymology: From Latin 'crepusculum' (twilight), from 'creper' (dusky).
exampleSentence: Deer are crepuscular, so you mostly see them at dawn and dusk.

definition: Twilight; dusk.
etymology: From Old English 'glomung,' related to 'glom' (twilight), of Germanic origin.
exampleSentence: We sat on the porch in the gloaming, not saying much.

definition: The soft glowing light from the sky when the sun is below the horizon.
etymology: From Middle English 'twi-' (two or half) and 'light,' suggesting the half-light between day and night.
exampleSentence: There's a particular twilight in early summer that I'd bottle if I could.

definition: The darker stage of twilight before night fully sets in.
etymology: From Old English 'dox,' meaning dark or dusky.
exampleSentence: The fireflies come out right at dusk.

definition: A partial shadow between full shadow and full light.
etymology: From Latin 'paene' (almost) and 'umbra' (shadow).
exampleSentence: During the eclipse, we stood in the strange chill of the penumbra.

definition: The fully shaded inner region of a shadow.
etymology: From Latin 'umbra,' meaning shade or shadow.
exampleSentence: The total eclipse passed right through our umbra.

definition: To outline or foreshadow vaguely.
etymology: From Latin 'adumbrare,' meaning to cast a shadow on, from 'ad-' (to) and 'umbra' (shadow).
exampleSentence: His opening remarks adumbrated a plan he never quite explained.

definition: To suggest or hint at something delicately.
etymology: From Latin 'intimare,' meaning to announce, from 'intimus' (innermost).
exampleSentence: She intimated that there might be a promotion coming.

definition: To suggest or hint at something unpleasant in an indirect way.
etymology: From Latin 'insinuare,' meaning to wind one's way in, from 'in-' (in) and 'sinuare' (to bend).
exampleSentence: He didn't accuse me — he just insinuated.

definition: To suggest or call attention to indirectly.
etymology: From Latin 'alludere,' meaning to play with, from 'ad-' (to) and 'ludere' (to play).
exampleSentence: She alluded to her past in interviews but never really explained it.

definition: To fail to give a true impression of something; to contradict.
etymology: From Old English 'beleogan,' meaning to deceive with lies, from 'be-' and 'leogan' (to lie).
exampleSentence: Her calm voice belied how nervous she really was.

definition: The principal front of a building, or a deceptive outward appearance.
etymology: From French 'facade,' from Italian 'facciata,' from 'faccia' (face).
exampleSentence: His cheerful facade was wearing thin by Friday.

definition: A thin decorative covering, or a superficial appearance.
etymology: From French 'fournir' (to furnish), via German 'Furnier,' first applied to thin layers of fine wood.
exampleSentence: Beneath his polished veneer was a guy who really wanted to talk about pigeons.

definition: A green or brown film on bronze, or an impression of age and history.
etymology: From Italian 'patina,' originally meaning a shallow dish, from Latin 'patina' (pan); the chemistry sense developed later.
exampleSentence: The leather chair has a wonderful patina from decades of use.

definition: A small remaining trace of something that once existed.
etymology: From Latin 'vestigium' (footprint or trace).
exampleSentence: There's not a vestige of his old accent left.

definition: A small remaining quantity of something.
etymology: From Old French 'remenant,' present participle of 'remenoir' (to remain), from Latin 'remanere.'
exampleSentence: The fabric store sells remnants by the pound.

definition: An object or custom surviving from an earlier time.
etymology: From Latin 'reliquiae,' meaning remains, from 'relinquere' (to leave behind).
exampleSentence: My grandpa's rotary phone is a relic, but it still works.

definition: A valuable object that has belonged to a family for generations.
etymology: From Middle English 'heir' and 'loom' (originally a tool or implement); the term meant a tool passed by inheritance.
exampleSentence: The pocket watch is the only real heirloom we have.

definition: An object thought to have magic powers and to bring good luck.
etymology: From Arabic 'tilsam,' from Greek 'telesma' (consecration ceremony), from 'telein' (to complete).
exampleSentence: He keeps a smooth river stone in his pocket as a talisman.

definition: A small object worn to protect against evil or harm.
etymology: From Latin 'amuletum,' of uncertain origin but used in classical times.
exampleSentence: She wore a tiny silver amulet she'd had since childhood.

definition: An event regarded as a sign of good or bad things to come.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin 'omen,' of uncertain origin but used in classical times.
exampleSentence: Seeing a heron on moving day felt like a good omen.

definition: A sign or omen of what is to come.
etymology: From Latin 'augurium,' the practice of an 'augur,' a priest who observed birds for omens.
exampleSentence: He took the rainbow as a private augury that the day would turn out fine.

definition: A person or thing that announces or signals the approach of another.
etymology: From Old French 'herbergere,' originally meaning a person who provided lodging, later one who went ahead to arrange shelter.
exampleSentence: The first robin is the classic harbinger of spring.

definition: A person or thing that comes before another of the same kind.
etymology: From Latin 'praecursor,' meaning a forerunner, from 'prae-' (before) and 'currere' (to run).
exampleSentence: That tiny shop was the precursor to the chain we know today.

definition: An introductory piece or event preceding something more important.
etymology: From medieval Latin 'praeludium,' from 'prae-' (before) and 'ludere' (to play).
exampleSentence: The light rain was just a prelude to the actual storm.

definition: An introduction to something more substantial; an opening move.
etymology: From Old French 'overture' (opening), from Latin 'apertura.'
exampleSentence: His handshake was an overture to a longer conversation.

definition: A separate introductory section of a work.
etymology: From Greek 'prologos,' from 'pro-' (before) and 'logos' (speech).
exampleSentence: Most readers skip the prologue, which is a shame.

definition: A concluding section added at the end of a work.
etymology: From Greek 'epilogos,' from 'epi-' (in addition) and 'logos' (speech).
exampleSentence: The epilogue tells you what happened to the characters years later.

definition: The final part of a story, when the strands are drawn together.
etymology: From French 'denouement,' from 'denouer' (to untie), from Latin 'nodus' (knot).
exampleSentence: The mystery had a satisfying denouement that didn't cheat.

definition: The most intense, exciting, or important point of something.
etymology: From Greek 'klimax,' meaning ladder, originally a rhetorical term for rising intensity.
exampleSentence: The climax of the parade was always the giant balloon.

definition: A gradual increase in loudness or intensity.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian, the present participle of 'crescere' (to grow), from Latin.
exampleSentence: The argument built to a crescendo, then suddenly went quiet.

definition: A rhythmic flow or modulation, especially of sound.
etymology: From Italian 'cadenza,' from Latin 'cadere' (to fall).
exampleSentence: He speaks with the easy cadence of someone who tells stories for a living.

definition: The character or quality of a musical sound or voice.
etymology: From French 'timbre,' originally meaning a small drum or bell, from Greek 'tympanon.'
exampleSentence: Her singing voice has a warm, smoky timbre.

definition: The quality of being deep, full, and reverberating; a deep significance.
etymology: From Latin 'resonare,' meaning to resound, from 're-' (back) and 'sonare' (to sound).
exampleSentence: That old folk song has new resonance for me now.

definition: To be repeated as an echo; to have continuing effects.
etymology: From Latin 'reverberare,' meaning to strike back, from 're-' (back) and 'verberare' (to lash).
exampleSentence: Her speech is still reverberating around the company.

definition: A pleasing view, especially one seen through a long narrow opening.
etymology: From Italian 'vista,' from 'vedere' (to see).
exampleSentence: From the top of the hill, the vista was worth every blister.

definition: An unbroken view of an entire surrounding area.
etymology: Coined in 1789 by painter Robert Barker from Greek 'pan-' (all) and 'horama' (sight), for his cylindrical paintings.
exampleSentence: From the rooftop you get a full panorama of the city.

definition: A group of motionless figures representing a scene; a striking picture.
etymology: From French 'tableau,' meaning a picture, from 'table' (table or board).
exampleSentence: The family at the table looked like a tableau out of a magazine.

definition: The dark outline of a person or object against a lighter background.
etymology: From the name of Etienne de Silhouette, an 18th-century French finance minister whose name became attached to cheap shadow portraits.
exampleSentence: His silhouette against the sunset is one of those pictures we keep on the fridge.

definition: The treatment of light and shade in drawing and painting.
etymology: From Italian, from 'chiaro' (light) and 'oscuro' (dark).
exampleSentence: The photograph had a beautiful chiaroscuro feel, almost painted.

definition: The emission of light not caused by heat.
etymology: From Latin 'lumen' (light) and the suffix '-escence' indicating a process.
exampleSentence: The fireflies gave the field a faint luminescence.

definition: Showing luminous colors that seem to change when seen from different angles.
etymology: From Latin 'iris' (rainbow), itself from Greek 'Iris,' the messenger goddess of the rainbow.
exampleSentence: The hummingbird's throat was iridescent green and ruby.

definition: Showing varying colors as an opal does.
etymology: From the gem 'opal,' from Sanskrit 'upala' (precious stone), via Greek and Latin.
exampleSentence: The morning sky was a soft opalescent pink.

definition: Having a luster like a pearl.
etymology: Combination of 'pearl' (from Latin 'perna') and the suffix '-escent.'
exampleSentence: They picked a pearlescent paint for the car that changes color in the sun.

definition: Light, thin, and delicate.
etymology: From Middle English 'gosesomer,' literally 'goose summer,' a name for a warm spell in autumn when spider webs covered the fields.
exampleSentence: Her dress was almost gossamer — you could see right through the sleeves.

definition: Light, delicate, and translucent.
etymology: From medieval Latin 'diaphanus,' from Greek 'diaphanes' (transparent), from 'dia-' (through) and 'phainein' (to show).
exampleSentence: The curtains were a diaphanous white that lit up at sunrise.

definition: Extremely delicate and light, in a way that seems not of this world.
etymology: From Greek 'aitherios,' from 'aither,' the upper pure air above the clouds.
exampleSentence: There was something ethereal about her singing voice.

definition: A feeling of reverential respect mixed with wonder.
etymology: From Old Norse 'agi,' meaning fear or terror.
exampleSentence: She watched the launch in genuine awe.

definition: Deep respect for someone or something.
etymology: From Latin 'reverentia,' from 'revereri' (to stand in awe of), from 're-' (intensive) and 'vereri' (to fear).
exampleSentence: He spoke of his old teacher with real reverence.

definition: Devotion to religion or strong belief.
etymology: From Latin 'pietas,' meaning dutifulness, from 'pius' (devout).
exampleSentence: Her piety was quiet but constant.

definition: Deeply religious or earnestly committed.
etymology: From Old French 'devot,' from Latin 'devotus,' past participle of 'devovere' (to dedicate).
exampleSentence: He's a devout fan of late-90s indie rock.

definition: Having or displaying passionate intensity.
etymology: From Latin 'fervere' (to boil).
exampleSentence: She wrote a fervent letter to the editor about the new zoning.

definition: Filled with or showing great emotion.
etymology: From Italian 'impassionare' (to be impassioned), from Latin 'pati' (to suffer).
exampleSentence: He gave an impassioned defense of public libraries.

definition: Showing strong feeling; forceful.
etymology: From Latin 'vehemens,' perhaps from 've-' (lacking) and 'mens' (mind), suggesting being carried away.
exampleSentence: Her denial was so vehement it almost convinced me of the opposite.

definition: Loud and harsh; insistent and unpleasant.
etymology: From Latin 'stridere' (to make a harsh sound).
exampleSentence: The debate got more strident as the night went on.

definition: High-sounding but with little meaning; inflated.
etymology: From 'bombast,' originally a soft material used to pad clothing, from Old French 'bombace' (cotton).
exampleSentence: His bombastic speeches don't really work in a small room.

definition: Impressive or magnificent, often pretentiously so.
etymology: From French 'grandiose,' from Italian 'grandioso,' from Latin 'grandis' (great).
exampleSentence: He has grandiose plans for the garage that he'll never carry out.

definition: Designed to impress or attract notice.
etymology: From Latin 'ostentare,' a frequentative of 'ostendere' (to show).
exampleSentence: The diamond ring was a little ostentatious for a Tuesday brunch.

definition: Tending to attract attention because of confidence and lively quality.
etymology: From French 'flamboyer' (to flame), from 'flambe' (flame); originally describing wavy, flame-like Gothic architecture.
exampleSentence: His flamboyant style is half the reason people watch his show.

definition: Attractive and impressive through being richly colorful or sumptuous.
etymology: From Latin 'resplendere,' meaning to shine brightly, from 're-' (intensive) and 'splendere' (to shine).
exampleSentence: The bride was resplendent in deep red.

definition: Impressively beautiful, elaborate, or extravagant.
etymology: From Latin 'magnificus,' from 'magnus' (great) and 'facere' (to make).
exampleSentence: That was a magnificent breakfast — I'll need a nap.

definition: Magnificent; very impressive.
etymology: From Latin 'splendidus,' from 'splendere' (to shine).
exampleSentence: It was a splendid morning for a walk along the river.

definition: Extremely beautiful and delicate.
etymology: From Latin 'exquisitus,' past participle of 'exquirere' (to search out), from 'ex-' (out) and 'quaerere' (to seek).
exampleSentence: The pastry was an exquisite little thing, almost too pretty to eat.

definition: In its original condition; perfectly clean.
etymology: From Latin 'pristinus,' meaning former or original.
exampleSentence: The book was sixty years old but pristine.

definition: Perfectly clean, neat, or tidy.
etymology: From Latin 'immaculatus,' from 'in-' (not) and 'macula' (spot or stain).
exampleSentence: His desk is immaculate, which is probably why he can't find anything.

definition: Translucently clear in meaning or expression.
etymology: From Latin 'pellucidus,' from 'per-' (through) and 'lucere' (to shine).
exampleSentence: She has a pellucid writing style — never a wasted word.

definition: Expressed clearly; easy to understand.
etymology: From Latin 'lucidus,' from 'lucere' (to shine).
exampleSentence: He was lucid right up to the end, telling stories the night before.

definition: Clear, logical, and convincing.
etymology: From Latin 'cogens,' present participle of 'cogere' (to compel), from 'co-' (together) and 'agere' (to drive).
exampleSentence: She made a cogent case for working from home on Fridays.

definition: Most noticeable or important.
etymology: From Latin 'saliens,' present participle of 'salire' (to leap).
exampleSentence: The most salient point of the report was buried on page nine.

definition: Relevant to a subject under consideration.
etymology: From Middle English 'germain' (closely related, akin), from Latin 'germanus' (of the same parents).
exampleSentence: That detail isn't really germane to what we're deciding.

definition: Very appropriate to a particular situation.
etymology: From French 'a propos,' literally 'to the purpose.'
exampleSentence: His comment was funny and surprisingly apropos.

definition: A statement accepted as established or self-evidently true.
etymology: From Greek 'axioma,' meaning 'that which is thought worthy,' from 'axios' (worthy).
exampleSentence: My uncle's life axiom is 'measure twice, cut once.'

definition: A proverb or short statement expressing a general truth.
etymology: From Latin 'adagium,' meaning a saying, of obscure origin.
exampleSentence: The old adage about early birds doesn't apply if you don't want worms.

definition: A concise observation that contains a general truth.
etymology: From Greek 'aphorismos,' meaning definition, from 'aphorizein' (to set apart).
exampleSentence: His talks are basically strung-together aphorisms about leadership.

definition: A short, pithy statement expressing a general rule of conduct.
etymology: From medieval Latin 'maxima propositio' (greatest premise), from 'maximus' (greatest).
exampleSentence: Her maxim was 'never trust a clean kitchen.'

definition: A statement that is obviously true and says nothing new.
etymology: Coined in the 18th century from 'true' plus the suffix '-ism.'
exampleSentence: That advice is a truism, but it's also correct.

definition: A remark used too often to be interesting or thoughtful.
etymology: From French 'platitude,' from 'plat' (flat), modeled on 'latitude.'
exampleSentence: At funerals you hear the same platitudes over and over.

definition: A short, witty saying.
etymology: From Greek 'epigramma,' meaning inscription, from 'epi-' (upon) and 'graphein' (to write).
exampleSentence: Wilde could turn out an epigram between sips of tea.

definition: A witty remark.
etymology: Coined in 1677 by John Dryden, blending 'witty' and 'criticism.'
exampleSentence: He has a witticism ready for every awkward silence.

definition: Quick, clever remarks exchanged in conversation.
etymology: From French 'repartie,' meaning a quick reply, from 'repartir' (to set off again).
exampleSentence: Their repartee at dinner is half the reason I keep coming back.

definition: Playful, friendly teasing exchanged between people.
etymology: Origin uncertain; recorded in the late 17th century, possibly slang.
exampleSentence: There's always good banter at the deli counter.

definition: Humorous or witty conversation.
etymology: From French 'badinage,' from 'badiner' (to joke), from Provencal 'badar' (to gape).
exampleSentence: The whole dinner was light badinage and no one wanted it to end.

definition: Light, mocking banter or teasing.
etymology: From French 'persiflage,' from 'persifler' (to mock), from 'per-' (through) and 'siffler' (to whistle).
exampleSentence: His persiflage about my haircut went on a little too long.

definition: The treatment of a serious matter with humor or lack of due respect.
etymology: From Latin 'levitas,' from 'levis' (light).
exampleSentence: A little levity at the wake actually helped.

definition: Amusement, especially expressed in laughter.
etymology: From Old English 'myrgth,' from 'myrige' (pleasant), of Germanic origin.
exampleSentence: The kitchen was full of mirth and the smell of cinnamon.

definition: Great delight, especially from one's own good fortune or another's misfortune.
etymology: From Old English 'gleo,' meaning entertainment or music.
exampleSentence: My son shouted with glee when the snow finally started falling.

definition: Feeling or expressing great happiness and triumph.
etymology: From Latin 'jubilare,' meaning to call out, possibly imitative.
exampleSentence: The team was jubilant in the locker room.

definition: Triumphantly happy.
etymology: From Latin 'exsultare,' a frequentative of 'exsilire' (to leap up), from 'ex-' (out) and 'salire' (to jump).
exampleSentence: She let out an exultant shout when the package finally arrived.

definition: Extremely happy and excited.
etymology: From Latin 'elatus,' meaning lifted up, past participle of 'efferre' (to carry out).
exampleSentence: He was elated about the new job for a solid week.

definition: Cheerful and optimistic.
etymology: From Spanish 'boyar' (to float), from Old French 'buie' (a buoy); the figurative sense developed in the 17th century.
exampleSentence: She's in a buoyant mood whenever it's gardening season.

definition: Cheerful and friendly.
etymology: From Latin 'jovialis,' relating to the planet Jupiter (Jove), whose influence was believed to produce happiness.
exampleSentence: Our jovial mailman knows every dog on the block by name.

definition: Friendly, good-natured, and easy to talk to.
etymology: From Latin 'affabilis,' from 'affari' (to speak to), from 'ad-' (to) and 'fari' (to speak).
exampleSentence: The new dentist is affable in a way that almost makes me forget I hate dentists.

definition: Friendly and cheerful.
etymology: From Latin 'genialis,' meaning festive or relating to the 'genius' (one's tutelary spirit).
exampleSentence: He's the genial host who makes sure no one is left out.

definition: Having a friendly and pleasant manner.
etymology: From Latin 'amicabilis,' from 'amicus' (friend).
exampleSentence: My new boss is amiable, but I haven't seen her in a tough situation yet.

definition: Warm and friendly.
etymology: From medieval Latin 'cordialis,' from Latin 'cor' (heart).
exampleSentence: Their handshake was cordial but a little stiff.

definition: Well meaning and kindly.
etymology: From Latin 'benevolens,' from 'bene' (well) and 'volens' (wishing).
exampleSentence: He gave me a benevolent smile and waved off the late fee.

definition: More generous than is usual or necessary.
etymology: From Latin 'munificus,' meaning bountiful, from 'munus' (gift) and 'facere' (to make).
exampleSentence: A munificent stranger paid the tab for the whole counter.

definition: Generous or forgiving, especially toward a rival.
etymology: From Latin 'magnanimus,' from 'magnus' (great) and 'animus' (soul).
exampleSentence: He was magnanimous in defeat, congratulating the winner first.

definition: Showing a selfless concern for the well-being of others.
etymology: Coined by Auguste Comte in 1830 from French 'autrui' (other people), from Latin 'alter' (other).
exampleSentence: His motives aren't entirely altruistic, but the food bank still benefits.

definition: Seeking to promote the welfare of others; generous.
etymology: From Greek 'philanthropos,' from 'phil-' (loving) and 'anthropos' (man).
exampleSentence: She turned a chunk of her fortune into a philanthropic foundation.

definition: The ability to understand and share the feelings of another.
etymology: Coined in 1908 to translate German 'Einfühlung' (feeling into), from Greek 'empatheia' (passion).
exampleSentence: He has the kind of empathy that makes strangers tell him things.

definition: Sympathetic concern for the sufferings of others.
etymology: From Latin 'compassio,' from 'com-' (with) and 'pati' (to suffer).
exampleSentence: She treats her patients with patience and compassion.

definition: Compassion shown toward someone one has the power to punish.
etymology: From Old French 'merci,' meaning pity or thanks, from Latin 'merces' (reward).
exampleSentence: The judge showed mercy and reduced the sentence.

definition: Mercy or leniency, especially toward an offender.
etymology: From Latin 'clementia,' from 'clemens' (mild).
exampleSentence: He's hoping for clemency given his clean record.

definition: Elegance of movement, or unmerited favor.
etymology: From Latin 'gratia,' meaning favor or thanks, from 'gratus' (pleasing).
exampleSentence: She handled the bad news with extraordinary grace.

definition: Graceful and elegant bearing; composure.
etymology: From Old French 'pois' (weight), from Latin 'pensum.'
exampleSentence: He answered the hostile question with complete poise.

definition: The state of being calm and self-controlled.
etymology: From Latin 'componere' (to put together), from 'com-' (together) and 'ponere' (to place).
exampleSentence: She lost her composure exactly once during the trial.

definition: Mental calmness and even-temperedness in difficult situations.
etymology: From Latin 'aequanimitas,' from 'aequus' (even) and 'animus' (mind).
exampleSentence: He accepted the diagnosis with surprising equanimity.

definition: Patient self-control and restraint under provocation.
etymology: Formed in the 16th century from 'forbear,' from Old English 'forberan' (to endure).
exampleSentence: It took every ounce of forbearance not to say what I was thinking.

definition: The capacity to accept delay or trouble without getting upset.
etymology: From Latin 'patientia,' from 'pati' (to suffer or bear).
exampleSentence: Sourdough teaches you patience whether you wanted to learn or not.

definition: Courage in pain or adversity.
etymology: From Latin 'fortitudo,' from 'fortis' (strong).
exampleSentence: The recovery took real fortitude over many months.

definition: A person's ability to cope well with difficulties.
etymology: A variant spelling of 'metal,' from Latin 'metallum'; the figurative sense developed in the 16th century.
exampleSentence: This week will really test her mettle.

definition: Courage and determination despite difficulty.
etymology: From Old English 'greot' (sand or gravel); the figurative sense of resolve developed in 19th-century American English.
exampleSentence: He doesn't have raw talent, but he has grit.

definition: Force of character, determination, or nerve.
etymology: From the brand name of a popular American soft drink introduced in 1885, said to give 'pep.'
exampleSentence: It takes some moxie to start a bakery during a recession.

definition: Bold, brash self-confidence; nerve.
etymology: Borrowed from Yiddish 'khutspe,' from Hebrew 'huspa' (insolence).
exampleSentence: She had the chutzpah to ask the CEO for his parking spot.

definition: The appearance of being true or real.
etymology: From Latin 'verisimilitudo,' from 'verisimilis' (probable), from 'verus' (true) and 'similis' (like).
exampleSentence: The movie's verisimilitude comes from filming on the real streets.

definition: Of undisputed origin; genuine.
etymology: From Greek 'authentikos,' meaning principal or genuine, from 'authentes' (one acting on one's own authority).
exampleSentence: That's an authentic 1960s diner, right down to the jukebox.

definition: Truly what something is said to be; sincere.
etymology: From Latin 'genuinus,' meaning native or natural, from 'genu' (knee) — a Roman father formally acknowledged his newborn by placing it on his knee.
exampleSentence: Her surprise was completely genuine.

definition: Genuine; real.
etymology: From Latin 'bona fide,' meaning in good faith, an ablative phrase.
exampleSentence: He's a bona fide expert on Renaissance armor.

definition: Self-evident; unquestionable.
etymology: From Greek 'axiomatikos,' from 'axioma' (something thought worthy).
exampleSentence: In our family it's axiomatic that you don't talk politics at Thanksgiving.

definition: Not able to be denied or disputed.
etymology: From Latin 'incontrovertibilis,' from 'in-' (not) and 'controvertere' (to turn against).
exampleSentence: The video provided incontrovertible proof.

definition: Leaving no doubt; unambiguous.
etymology: From Latin 'aequivocus' (of equal voice), prefixed with 'un-' (not).
exampleSentence: Her answer was unequivocal — she was not moving.

definition: Expressing something forcibly and clearly.
etymology: From Greek 'emphatikos,' from 'emphainein' (to indicate), from 'en-' (in) and 'phainein' (to show).
exampleSentence: He gave an emphatic no to the whole proposal.

definition: Unambiguously explicit and direct.
etymology: From late Latin 'categoricus,' from Greek 'kategorikos,' from 'kategoria' (accusation or category).
exampleSentence: She issued a categorical denial within an hour.

definition: Inclined to lay down principles as incontrovertibly true.
etymology: From Greek 'dogmatikos,' from 'dogma' (opinion).
exampleSentence: He's dogmatic about coffee in a way I find a little tiring.

definition: Conforming to what is generally accepted.
etymology: From Greek 'orthodoxos,' from 'orthos' (straight or correct) and 'doxa' (opinion).
exampleSentence: That's not the orthodox way to make a souffle, but it works for him.

definition: Not conforming to accepted standards or beliefs.
etymology: From Greek 'heterodoxos,' from 'heteros' (other) and 'doxa' (opinion).
exampleSentence: Her heterodox views on monetary policy keep getting her speaking gigs.

definition: A person who attacks cherished beliefs or institutions.
etymology: From Greek 'eikonoklastes,' meaning image-breaker, originally those who destroyed religious icons in 8th-century Byzantium.
exampleSentence: Every field needs at least one good iconoclast.

definition: An unorthodox or independent-minded person.
etymology: From Samuel A. Maverick, a 19th-century Texas rancher who refused to brand his cattle, so unbranded strays came to be called 'mavericks.'
exampleSentence: He's a maverick on the board — he votes how he wants.

definition: A person who deserts a cause or organization.
etymology: From Spanish 'renegado,' from medieval Latin 'renegatus,' past participle of 'renegare' (to renounce).
exampleSentence: A small group of renegades broke from the main party.

definition: The leading position in a new development or trend.
etymology: From Old French 'avant-garde,' literally 'fore-guard,' the soldiers at the front of an army.
exampleSentence: That little studio is the vanguard of the new sound.

definition: New and experimental, especially in the arts.
etymology: Borrowed from French 'avant-garde,' originally a military term for advance troops.
exampleSentence: Her work is avant-garde even by Berlin standards.

definition: Living an unconventional, artistic lifestyle.
etymology: From French 'bohemien,' originally meaning Gypsy (mistakenly believed to come from Bohemia), then transferred to artists living unconventionally.
exampleSentence: Their apartment has a charming bohemian vibe.

definition: Unconventional and slightly strange.
etymology: From Greek 'ekkentros,' meaning out of the center, from 'ek-' (out of) and 'kentron' (center).
exampleSentence: My eccentric aunt has a collection of antique typewriters.

definition: Relating to a person's distinctive way of behaving or thinking.
etymology: From Greek 'idiosynkrasia,' from 'idios' (own) and 'synkrasis' (mixture).
exampleSentence: He has an idiosyncratic way of organizing his bookshelf — by mood.

definition: Characterized by peculiar or unexpected traits.
etymology: From 'quirk' (a peculiar feature or twist), of unknown origin, recorded in the 1500s.
exampleSentence: It's a quirky little cafe with handwritten menus.

definition: Playfully quaint or fanciful.
etymology: From 'whim,' of obscure origin but possibly from 'whim-wham,' a 16th-century word for a fanciful object.
exampleSentence: The illustrations have a whimsical, storybook feel.

definition: Given to sudden and unaccountable changes of mood or behavior.
etymology: From Italian 'capriccio,' originally meaning a sudden start or whim, possibly from 'capo' (head) and 'riccio' (hedgehog), suggesting hair standing on end.
exampleSentence: The weather has been capricious lately — coat, no coat, coat.

definition: Subject to sudden or unpredictable changes of mood.
etymology: From Latin 'mercurialis,' relating to the god Mercury, who was known for swift, changeable nature.
exampleSentence: He's brilliant but mercurial — never quite sure which version of him you'll get.

definition: Liable to change rapidly and unpredictably.
etymology: From Latin 'volatilis,' meaning flying or fleeting, from 'volare' (to fly).
exampleSentence: The stock market has been volatile all week.

definition: Having a lot of space inside; roomy.
etymology: From Latin 'capax,' from 'capere' (to take or hold).
exampleSentence: She carries a capacious tote that seems to contain everything.

definition: Occupying or containing much space; large.
etymology: From Latin 'voluminosus,' from 'volumen' (a roll of writing).
exampleSentence: He arrived with voluminous notes for a thirty-minute meeting.

definition: Abundant in supply or quantity.
etymology: From Latin 'copiosus,' from 'copia' (plenty).
exampleSentence: She takes copious notes at every meeting.

definition: An excess or overabundance of something.
etymology: From Greek 'plethora,' meaning fullness, originally a medical term for excess of blood, from 'plethein' (to be full).
exampleSentence: There's a plethora of weather apps that all say the same thing.

definition: An excessive amount of something.
etymology: From Old French 'sorfait,' meaning excess, from Latin 'super-' (over) and 'facere' (to do).
exampleSentence: After the holidays I have a surfeit of cookies.

definition: An excessive supply of something.
etymology: From Middle English 'glouten,' to swallow greedily, of obscure origin.
exampleSentence: There's a glut of streaming services now.

definition: A scarcity or lack of something.
etymology: From Middle English 'derthe,' meaning costliness, from 'der' (dear or precious).
exampleSentence: There's a dearth of good Thai food in this neighborhood.

definition: The presence of something only in small amounts; scarcity.
etymology: From Latin 'paucitas,' from 'paucus' (few).
exampleSentence: There's a paucity of evidence either way.

definition: Thinly dispersed or scattered.
etymology: From Latin 'sparsus,' past participle of 'spargere' (to scatter).
exampleSentence: Attendance was sparse for the early show.

definition: Lacking in quantity or quality.
etymology: From Old French 'megre,' from Latin 'macer' (thin).
exampleSentence: They survived on meager rations for the long bus ride.

definition: Sparing or economical with money or food.
etymology: From Latin 'frugalis,' from 'frugi' (useful or worthy), originally meaning fitting for fruit.
exampleSentence: She's frugal in small ways and generous in big ones.

definition: Using money and other resources carefully and not wastefully.
etymology: From Old Norse 'thrift' (prosperity), from 'thrifa' (to grasp or thrive).
exampleSentence: He's thrifty without being miserly, which is a fine line.

definition: Unwilling to spend money or use resources; stingy.
etymology: From Latin 'parsimonia,' from 'parcere' (to spare).
exampleSentence: The restaurant is parsimonious with the bread basket.

definition: Of or characteristic of a miser; stingy.
etymology: From 'miser,' from Latin 'miser' (wretched), the noun sense developing in the 16th century.
exampleSentence: He's miserly with praise but generous with criticism.

definition: Extreme greed for wealth or material gain.
etymology: From Latin 'avaritia,' from 'avarus' (greedy).
exampleSentence: The whole scandal traced back to plain old avarice.

definition: To desire something belonging to another.
etymology: From Old French 'coveitier,' from Latin 'cupiditas' (desire), from 'cupere' (to desire).
exampleSentence: I covet my neighbor's herb garden, I'll admit it.

definition: To have an intense longing for something.
etymology: From Old English 'giernan,' meaning to desire, of Germanic origin.
exampleSentence: After two weeks of rain, I yearn for sunlight.

definition: To feel a strong desire for or to do something.
etymology: Probably from Dutch 'hunkeren,' related to 'hangen' (to hang), suggesting lingering.
exampleSentence: I've been hankering for my grandma's lasagna all week.

definition: To feel a powerful desire for something.
etymology: From Old English 'crafian,' meaning to demand, of Germanic origin.
exampleSentence: Around 3 p.m. I always crave something salty.

definition: To suffer a lingering, often nostalgic desire.
etymology: From Old English 'pinian,' meaning to torment, from Latin 'poena' (penalty).
exampleSentence: He pines for the snow days of his childhood.

definition: To have a strong wish or desire.
etymology: From Old English 'langian,' related to 'lang' (long), suggesting time stretching.
exampleSentence: She's longed for a real porch since she moved into the apartment.

definition: Having or showing a great desire to possess something, especially something belonging to someone else.
etymology: From Old French 'coveitos,' from 'coveitier' (to covet).
exampleSentence: He gave my new bike a covetous look.

definition: Feeling resentful longing aroused by another's possessions.
etymology: From Old French 'envieus,' from Latin 'invidiosus,' from 'invidere' (to look upon with malice).
exampleSentence: I'm envious of anyone who can actually sleep on planes.

definition: Feeling resentment toward someone because of their advantages.
etymology: From Old French 'jelous,' from late Latin 'zelosus,' from Greek 'zelos' (ardor or rivalry).
exampleSentence: I'm jealous of his commute — a twelve-minute walk through a park.

definition: Bitter indignation at being treated unfairly.
etymology: From French 'ressentiment,' from 'ressentir' (to feel back), from 're-' and 'sentir' (to feel).
exampleSentence: Old resentment has a way of leaking out at family dinners.

definition: Long-lasting bitterness or resentment.
etymology: From Old French 'rancor,' from late Latin 'rancor,' meaning rankness, from 'rancere' (to stink).
exampleSentence: They divorced amicably — no rancor, even a little fondness.

definition: Bitterness or sharpness in temper, manner, or speech.
etymology: From Latin 'acrimonia,' from 'acer' (sharp).
exampleSentence: The negotiations dragged on with growing acrimony.

definition: Strong hostility.
etymology: From Latin 'animositas,' meaning spirit or courage, later coming to mean hostility, from 'animus' (mind, spirit).
exampleSentence: There's no animosity between them — they just don't have much to say.

definition: The state of being actively opposed or hostile to someone.
etymology: From Old French 'enemistie,' from late Latin 'inimicitia,' from 'inimicus' (enemy).
exampleSentence: The enmity between the two coaches is older than most of the players.

definition: A prolonged and bitter quarrel between two parties.
etymology: From Old French 'feide,' of Germanic origin, related to Old English 'faehth' (enmity).
exampleSentence: Their family feud started over a borrowed lawn mower.

definition: A long, bitter quarrel or campaign waged by one person against another.
etymology: From Italian 'vendetta,' from Latin 'vindicta' (vengeance).
exampleSentence: My cat has a personal vendetta against the vacuum.

definition: To restore friendly relations between people.
etymology: From Latin 'reconciliare,' from 're-' (back) and 'conciliare' (to bring together).
exampleSentence: It took years for the brothers to reconcile.

definition: To make someone less angry or hostile.
etymology: From Latin 'placare,' meaning to calm or appease.
exampleSentence: He tried to placate the customer with a free dessert.

definition: To pacify or soothe someone by giving in to demands.
etymology: From Old French 'apeser,' literally 'to bring to peace,' from 'a-' (to) and 'pais' (peace).
exampleSentence: They added a vegetarian option to appease the family.

definition: To soothe or appease.
etymology: From Latin 'mollificare,' from 'mollis' (soft) and 'facere' (to make).
exampleSentence: A long apology email did not mollify her.

definition: To make an unpleasant feeling less intense.
etymology: From Old French 'assouagier,' from Latin 'ad-' (to) and 'suavis' (sweet).
exampleSentence: A bowl of soup can assuage a lot of small sorrows.

definition: To make a problem less severe.
etymology: From late Latin 'alleviare,' from 'ad-' (to) and 'levis' (light).
exampleSentence: A nap alleviates almost any minor grievance.

definition: To make something better.
etymology: From French 'ameliorer,' from Latin 'melior' (better).
exampleSentence: Better lighting can really ameliorate a cramped office.

definition: To make less severe or painful.
etymology: From Latin 'mitigare,' from 'mitis' (gentle) and 'agere' (to drive).
exampleSentence: They added a porch roof to mitigate the afternoon sun.

definition: To become less intense or widespread.
etymology: From Old French 'abatre,' meaning to beat down, from Latin 'ad-' (to) and 'battere' (to beat).
exampleSentence: The storm finally abated around midnight.

definition: To decrease in size, strength, or importance.
etymology: From Old English 'wanian,' meaning to lessen, of Germanic origin.
exampleSentence: My enthusiasm for yoga waxes and wanes with the weather.

definition: To gradually increase in size or strength.
etymology: From Old English 'weaxan,' meaning to grow, of Germanic origin.
exampleSentence: Her interest in mushrooms has waxed considerably this autumn.

definition: To begin to grow or increase rapidly.
etymology: From Old French 'burjon' (a bud), of uncertain origin.
exampleSentence: The neighborhood has burgeoned since the new park opened.

definition: To grow or develop in a healthy or vigorous way.
etymology: From Old French 'floriss-,' stem of 'florir' (to blossom), from Latin 'florere.'
exampleSentence: The basil flourished on the kitchen windowsill.

definition: To prosper or flourish.
etymology: From Old Norse 'thrifask,' meaning to grasp for oneself, from 'thrifa' (to grasp).
exampleSentence: Some plants thrive on neglect, which suits me.

definition: To succeed in material terms or be fortunate.
etymology: From Latin 'prosperare,' from 'prosperus' (favorable).
exampleSentence: Their little bakery has prospered since the move.

definition: To struggle or move clumsily; to be in difficulty.
etymology: Probably a blend of 'founder' and 'blunder,' formed in the late 16th century.
exampleSentence: I floundered for an answer when she asked about my five-year plan.

definition: To fail or come to nothing; to sink.
etymology: From Old French 'fondrer,' meaning to send to the bottom, from 'fond' (bottom).
exampleSentence: The deal foundered on a single clause about parking.

definition: To become weak or feeble; to suffer from being kept in unpleasant conditions.
etymology: From Old French 'languir,' from Latin 'languere' (to be weak).
exampleSentence: The bill has languished in committee for months.

definition: To cease to flow or develop.
etymology: From Latin 'stagnatum,' past participle of 'stagnare,' from 'stagnum' (standing water).
exampleSentence: His career has stagnated, but he says he doesn't mind.

definition: To gradually decline in effectiveness or vigor due to disuse.
etymology: From Greek 'atrophia,' from 'a-' (not) and 'trephein' (to feed).
exampleSentence: His French has atrophied since college.

definition: To become dry and shrunken; to fade.
etymology: From Middle English 'widren,' a variant of 'wedren' (to expose to weather).
exampleSentence: The orchid withered the moment I got it home.

definition: To become wrinkled and contracted, especially due to loss of moisture.
etymology: Origin uncertain; recorded in the 16th century, possibly of Scandinavian origin.
exampleSentence: The leftover salad had shriveled overnight.

definition: To make something extremely dry, especially due to heat.
etymology: From Middle English 'perchen,' possibly from Old French 'percher' (to perch) or via 'parchment.'
exampleSentence: By July the lawn was completely parched.

definition: Uncomfortably hot.
etymology: From Middle English 'swelten' (to faint from heat), from Old English 'sweltan' (to die).
exampleSentence: It was a sweltering August afternoon and the AC had quit.

definition: Pleasantly warm.
etymology: From 'balm,' a soothing ointment, from Greek 'balsamon.'
exampleSentence: It was a balmy evening, perfect for walking home.

definition: Mild in climate or temperament; self-restrained.
etymology: From Latin 'temperatus,' past participle of 'temperare' (to mix or moderate).
exampleSentence: He has a famously temperate disposition for a goalie.

definition: Mild, especially of weather; merciful.
etymology: From Latin 'clemens,' meaning mild, of uncertain origin.
exampleSentence: They had remarkably clement weather for the entire trip.

definition: Active and energetic; cold but invigorating.
etymology: Recorded in the late 16th century, perhaps from French 'brusque' (lively).
exampleSentence: It was a brisk fall morning that made you want to walk fast.

definition: Fresh and invigorating, especially of cold air.
etymology: From 'brace,' meaning to make strong or steady, from Old French 'bracier' (to embrace).
exampleSentence: A bracing swim before breakfast set the tone for the whole day.

definition: Firm, dry, and brittle; pleasantly cold and clear.
etymology: From Old English 'crisp,' meaning curly, from Latin 'crispus.'
exampleSentence: There was that first really crisp morning when you knew summer was done.

definition: Covered with frost; cold in manner.
etymology: From Old English 'forst' plus '-y,' the figurative sense developing in the 19th century.
exampleSentence: She gave me a frosty hello and went back to her crossword.

definition: Extremely cold; extremely slow.
etymology: From Latin 'glacialis,' from 'glacies' (ice).
exampleSentence: The pace at the DMV was, as always, glacial.

definition: Very hot and dry; full of intense emotion.
etymology: From Latin 'torridus,' from 'torrere' (to parch).
exampleSentence: They had a torrid summer fling that fizzled by Labor Day.

definition: Having little or no rain; dry.
etymology: From Latin 'aridus,' from 'arere' (to be dry).
exampleSentence: The conversation was arid — both of us just being polite.

definition: Green with vegetation.
etymology: Formed in the 17th century from 'verdure' (green vegetation), from Latin 'viridis.'
exampleSentence: The verdurous yard was an oasis on a sweltering block.

definition: Growing luxuriantly; rich and dense.
etymology: Recorded in the late 15th century, perhaps an alteration of obsolete 'lash' (soft).
exampleSentence: The garden was lush after a wet June.

definition: The quality or state of being green and lush.
etymology: Formed in the 17th century from 'verdant,' from Old French 'verdoyant,' from Latin 'viridis' (green).
exampleSentence: The hills regained their verdancy within days of the storm.

definition: A piece of grassland, especially used for hay.
etymology: From Old English 'maed,' related to 'mowan' (to mow).
exampleSentence: There's a meadow behind the school full of late-summer wildflowers.

definition: An open space in a forest.
etymology: Recorded in the 16th century, possibly related to 'glad' in the obsolete sense of bright.
exampleSentence: We had lunch in a sunny glade where the trees thinned out.

definition: A small valley, especially one with trees.
etymology: From Old English 'dell,' of Germanic origin, related to 'dale.'
exampleSentence: There's a quiet dell behind the cabin where the deer like to graze.

definition: A small group of trees.
etymology: From Old French 'copeiz,' meaning a cut wood, from 'couper' (to cut).
exampleSentence: A copse of birches stood at the edge of the field.

definition: A dense group of bushes or trees.
etymology: From Old English 'thiccet,' from 'thicce' (thick).
exampleSentence: The rabbit disappeared into the thicket before we could blink.

definition: A dense growth of shrubs and other plants under trees.
etymology: Formed in the 17th century from 'under' and 'growth.'
exampleSentence: The undergrowth was so thick we had to turn back.

definition: Prickly scrambling shrubs, especially blackberries.
etymology: From Old English 'bremel,' from 'brom' (broom), of Germanic origin.
exampleSentence: The brambles at the property line are full of blackberries every August.

definition: A long narrow trench made by a plow; a deep wrinkle.
etymology: From Old English 'furh,' of Germanic origin.
exampleSentence: There was a deep furrow in his brow that didn't go away.

definition: A small stream.
etymology: Probably from Low German 'rille' or Dutch 'ril,' both meaning a small channel.
exampleSentence: A little rill ran along the side of the path.

definition: A small stream.
etymology: From Old English 'broc,' of Germanic origin.
exampleSentence: There's a brook at the bottom of the field that never dries up.

definition: A small stream or inlet.
etymology: From Middle English 'crike,' from Old Norse 'kriki' (a nook).
exampleSentence: We hunted for crayfish in the creek behind the house.

definition: The tidal mouth of a large river.
etymology: From Latin 'aestuarium,' from 'aestus' (tide).
exampleSentence: Birds gather at the estuary every spring.

definition: A river or stream flowing into a larger river or lake.
etymology: From Latin 'tributarius,' from 'tributum' (tribute), from 'tribuere' (to pay).
exampleSentence: The Mohawk is a tributary of the Hudson.

definition: The junction of two rivers; a coming together of people or things.
etymology: From Latin 'confluentia,' from 'confluere' (to flow together).
exampleSentence: The festival is a confluence of food, music, and bad poetry.

definition: A particular point in events or time.
etymology: From Latin 'junctura,' from 'jungere' (to join).
exampleSentence: At this juncture, I'd recommend ordering dessert.

definition: A turning point in events or affairs.
etymology: A 19th-century English coinage modeled on German 'Wasserscheide,' meaning the line dividing two drainage basins.
exampleSentence: That book was a watershed in how I thought about food.

definition: An important event in the development of something.
etymology: Originally a literal stone marker showing distance along a road, with the figurative sense developing in the 19th century.
exampleSentence: Her first published essay was a real milestone.

definition: A standard or point of reference against which things are compared.
etymology: Originally a surveyor's mark cut into a wall to support a leveling staff, recorded in the 19th century.
exampleSentence: Her grandmother's pie is the benchmark every other pie fails to meet.

definition: A standard or criterion by which something is judged.
etymology: Originally a stone used to test the purity of gold by the streak it left when scratched.
exampleSentence: Honesty is his touchstone — everything else flows from that.

definition: A standard used for comparison or measurement.
etymology: Originally a literal measuring stick one yard long, with the figurative sense developing in the late 19th century.
exampleSentence: Speed isn't the only yardstick for a good runner.

definition: A person or thing seen as a perfect example.
etymology: From Italian 'paragone,' meaning a touchstone, from Greek 'parakonan' (to sharpen against).
exampleSentence: He's not exactly a paragon of organization.

definition: A perfect example of a quality or type.
etymology: From Greek 'epitome,' meaning summary, from 'epitemnein' (to cut short).
exampleSentence: This neighborhood is the epitome of unhurried living.

definition: A typical or original example of a person or thing.
etymology: From Greek 'arkhetypon,' from 'arkhe-' (primitive) and 'tupos' (type).
exampleSentence: He plays the archetype of the wise old mentor.

definition: A first model from which others are developed.
etymology: From Greek 'prototupon,' from 'protos' (first) and 'tupos' (type).
exampleSentence: The prototype was held together with duct tape.

definition: A typical example or pattern of something.
etymology: From Greek 'paradeigma,' from 'paradeiknunai' (to show side by side).
exampleSentence: The shop is a paradigm of how a small business should be run.

definition: A dominant or recurring idea in an artistic work.
