etymology: From French 'motif,' meaning motive or theme, from Latin 'motivus' (moving).
exampleSentence: There's a moth motif running through her embroidery.

definition: A recurring theme associated with a particular person or idea.
etymology: Borrowed from German 'Leitmotiv,' literally 'leading motive,' coined for Wagner's operas.
exampleSentence: Loneliness is a leitmotif in his early films.

definition: Made up of varied parts or types.
etymology: Recorded in the late 14th century, of uncertain origin, originally describing the variegated clothing of jesters.
exampleSentence: It was a motley crew at the open mic — but a generous audience.

definition: Drawing from a wide range of sources.
etymology: From Greek 'eklektikos,' from 'eklegein' (to pick out).
exampleSentence: Her playlist is eclectic — Bach to bluegrass to bossa nova.

definition: A confused mixture.
etymology: An alteration of 'hotchpotch,' from Old French 'hochepot,' a kind of stew.
exampleSentence: The shelf is a hodgepodge of paperbacks and seed packets.

definition: A buffet offering a variety of dishes; a wide range of something.
etymology: Borrowed from Swedish, from 'smörgås' (open sandwich) and 'bord' (table).
exampleSentence: The fair offered a smorgasbord of fried food.

definition: A varied mixture of people or things.
etymology: From Old French 'medlee,' meaning a fight or mixture, from Latin 'misculare' (to mix).
exampleSentence: The band closed with a medley of their early hits.

definition: A collection of various items.
etymology: From Latin 'miscellanea,' meaning a mixture, from 'miscellus' (mixed).
exampleSentence: That drawer is a miscellany of batteries, takeout menus, and old keys.

definition: Various; of different kinds.
etymology: From Old English 'syndrig,' meaning separate or special.
exampleSentence: He brought sundry gifts from his travels.

definition: A mixture of dried petals and spices used to scent a room; a varied mixture.
etymology: From French 'pot-pourri,' literally 'rotten pot,' originally a stew of mixed meats.
exampleSentence: There was a bowl of homemade potpourri by the front door.

definition: A holy place or sanctuary; something held sacred.
etymology: From Old English 'haligdom,' from 'halig' (holy) and the suffix '-dom.'
exampleSentence: His grandfather's woodshop was a kind of halidom to him.

definition: Of long ago or former times.
etymology: From Old English 'geara,' meaning formerly, related to 'gear' (year).
exampleSentence: In days of yore, you'd actually have to fold a paper map.

definition: The ancient past, especially the time before the Middle Ages.
etymology: From Latin 'antiquitas,' from 'antiquus' (ancient).
exampleSentence: She fell in love with antiquity on her first trip to Rome.

definition: Accorded great respect because of age or wisdom.
etymology: From Latin 'venerabilis,' from 'venerari' (to revere).
exampleSentence: The venerable bartender knew every regular's drink.

definition: Greatly revered, especially by tradition.
etymology: From Old English 'halgian,' meaning to make holy, from 'halig' (holy).
exampleSentence: Fenway is hallowed ground to a certain kind of fan.

definition: Connected with God or considered worthy of reverence.
etymology: From Latin 'sacrare,' meaning to consecrate, from 'sacer' (holy).
exampleSentence: Sunday morning coffee is a sacred ritual in this house.

definition: A sacred place, or a person's private refuge.
etymology: From Latin 'sanctum,' neuter of 'sanctus' (holy).
exampleSentence: The garden shed is his sanctum.

definition: A condition of being safe from danger or trouble.
etymology: From Latin 'refugium,' from 're-' (back) and 'fugere' (to flee).
exampleSentence: The library has always been her refuge.

definition: A place of safety or refuge.
etymology: From Old English 'haefen,' meaning a harbor, of Germanic origin.
exampleSentence: Their porch is a haven on summer evenings.

definition: A place of refuge or safety.
etymology: From Latin 'sanctuarium,' from 'sanctus' (holy).
exampleSentence: The little bookshop felt like a sanctuary from the city outside.

definition: A corner or recess that offers seclusion or security.
etymology: From Middle English 'nok,' of obscure origin, possibly Scandinavian.
exampleSentence: There's a perfect reading nook by the upstairs window.

definition: A recess in a wall or a part of a room set back from the rest.
etymology: From French 'alcove,' from Spanish 'alcoba,' from Arabic 'al-qubba' (the vault).
exampleSentence: She turned the alcove into a tiny library.

definition: A distinct area enclosed within a larger one.
etymology: From French 'enclave,' from 'enclaver' (to enclose), from Latin 'in-' and 'clavis' (key).
exampleSentence: That block is a Portuguese enclave in the middle of the city.

definition: A small settlement, generally smaller than a village.
etymology: From Old French 'hamelet,' a diminutive of 'ham' (village), of Germanic origin.
exampleSentence: They ended up in a tiny hamlet with one bar and no signal.

definition: A house, especially a farmhouse, and its land.
etymology: From Old English 'hamstede,' from 'ham' (home) and 'stede' (place).
exampleSentence: The old homestead still has Grandma's hand pump out back.

definition: A house or home.
etymology: From Old English 'abad,' past participle of 'abidan' (to abide).
exampleSentence: Welcome to my humble abode — please ignore the laundry.

definition: A house or place of residence.
etymology: From Old English 'dwellan,' meaning to lead astray or linger.
exampleSentence: Each dwelling on the block has its own quirky paint color.

definition: The floor of a fireplace; the home as a symbol of family life.
etymology: From Old English 'heorth,' of Germanic origin.
exampleSentence: The hearth was the warmest spot in the whole drafty house.

definition: The area around a fireplace, evoking warmth and intimacy.
etymology: Formed from 'hearth' (Old English 'heorth') and 'side.'
exampleSentence: Stories at the hearthside were a winter tradition.

definition: Giving a feeling of warmth and comfort.
etymology: Recorded in 18th-century Scots, of obscure origin, possibly Scandinavian.
exampleSentence: It's a cozy little bookstore with cats and good lighting.

definition: Cozy and comfortable.
etymology: Originally a 16th-century nautical term meaning trim or compact, of obscure origin.
exampleSentence: The kids were snug in their bunks while the rain hit the roof.

definition: A quality of coziness and contentment.
etymology: Borrowed from Danish, from Old Norse 'hyggja' (to think or take comfort).
exampleSentence: There's a particular hygge to candlelight and wool socks.

definition: Satisfied to the full; gratified.
etymology: From Latin 'satiare,' from 'satis' (enough).
exampleSentence: Sated and slightly sleepy, we walked back through the park.

definition: Filled or well-supplied with something.
etymology: From Latin 'repletus,' past participle of 'replere' (to fill up).
exampleSentence: The menu was replete with things I'd never seen before.

definition: Splendid and expensive-looking.
etymology: From Latin 'sumptuosus,' from 'sumptus' (expense).
exampleSentence: They served a sumptuous spread for a Wednesday lunch.

definition: Ostentatiously rich and luxurious.
etymology: From Latin 'opulentus,' from 'opes' (wealth).
exampleSentence: The lobby is a little too opulent for a community college.

definition: Sumptuously rich, elaborate, or luxurious.
etymology: From Old French 'lavasse,' meaning a downpour, from 'laver' (to wash).
exampleSentence: She threw a lavish party for her parents' anniversary.

definition: Lacking restraint in spending money or using resources.
etymology: From medieval Latin 'extravagans,' from 'extra-' (outside) and 'vagari' (to wander).
exampleSentence: His one extravagant habit is fountain pens.

definition: Spending money or using resources freely and recklessly.
etymology: From Latin 'prodigus,' from 'prodigere' (to drive away or squander).
exampleSentence: He was prodigal with compliments at the company holiday party.

definition: Recklessly extravagant.
etymology: From Latin 'profligatus,' past participle of 'profligare' (to ruin).
exampleSentence: They were profligate with butter, and I respected it.

definition: Extreme poverty.
etymology: From Latin 'penuria,' meaning scarcity, possibly related to 'paene' (almost).
exampleSentence: He grew up in real penury and never quite let himself enjoy spending.

definition: Without the basic necessities of life.
etymology: From Latin 'destitutus,' past participle of 'destituere' (to forsake).
exampleSentence: The charity feeds destitute families through the winter.

definition: To make poor; to deprive of strength or richness.
etymology: From Old French 'empoveriss-,' stem of 'empoverir,' from 'em-' and 'povre' (poor).
exampleSentence: Years of bad soil management had impoverished the land.

definition: The state of being extremely dirty and unpleasant.
etymology: From Latin 'squalor,' from 'squalere' (to be filthy).
exampleSentence: The kitchen, after the dinner party, was a state of cheerful squalor.

definition: Involving immoral or dishonorable actions; dirty.
etymology: From Latin 'sordidus,' from 'sordes' (dirt).
exampleSentence: The whole sordid story came out at the deposition.

definition: Covered in dirt; grubby.
etymology: From 'grime,' a 16th-century word probably of Low German origin.
exampleSentence: My fingers were grimy from rummaging around the engine.

definition: Dark and gloomy, especially due to thick mist; obscure.
etymology: From Middle English 'mirk,' from Old Norse 'myrkr' (dark).
exampleSentence: The funding sources were murky at best.

definition: Not discovered or known about; not clearly expressed.
etymology: From Latin 'obscurus,' meaning dark, from 'ob-' (over) and 'scurus' (covered).
exampleSentence: He has an obscure but devoted following online.

definition: Little known; abstruse.
etymology: From Latin 'reconditus,' past participle of 'recondere' (to put away).
exampleSentence: His specialty is some recondite branch of medieval law.

definition: Difficult to understand; obscure.
etymology: From Latin 'abstrusus,' past participle of 'abstrudere' (to push away).
exampleSentence: The instructions managed to be both abstruse and patronizing.

definition: To restore to a good or working state.
etymology: Formed in the 20th century from 're-' and 'condition.'
exampleSentence: He reconditioned the old radio and now it plays as well as new.

definition: To renovate and redecorate something.
etymology: From 're-' and obsolete 'furbish' (to polish), from Old French 'furbir.'
exampleSentence: They refurbished the diner without ruining what made it good.

definition: To bring back to a former condition.
etymology: From Latin 'restaurare,' to renew or rebuild.
exampleSentence: They restored the old church into a community center.

definition: To restore to consciousness or vigor.
etymology: From Latin 'revivere,' from 're-' (again) and 'vivere' (to live).
exampleSentence: Coffee can sometimes revive me, sometimes not.

definition: To make someone or something look or feel younger.
etymology: Formed in the 19th century from Latin 're-' and 'juvenis' (young).
exampleSentence: A long weekend can rejuvenate a tired marriage.

definition: To give strength or energy to.
etymology: From Latin 'in-' (into) and 'vigor' (force or energy).
exampleSentence: A cold swim will invigorate you for the rest of the morning.

definition: To shock or excite someone into taking action.
etymology: Named after Italian scientist Luigi Galvani, who in the late 1700s caused frog legs to twitch with electricity.
exampleSentence: The news galvanized the neighborhood into action.

definition: To excite or thrill someone.
etymology: Formed in the 17th century from 'electric' and the verb-forming suffix '-ify,' from Greek 'elektron' (amber).
exampleSentence: Her opening line electrified the whole room.

definition: A sudden feeling of intense excitement or pleasure.
etymology: From Middle English 'thrillen,' to pierce, an alteration of Old English 'thyrlian.'
exampleSentence: There's a particular thrill to a roller coaster you haven't ridden in years.

definition: A sudden, brief feeling of excitement or fear; a shiver.
etymology: From French 'frisson,' meaning a shiver, from Latin 'frigere' (to be cold).
exampleSentence: There's a frisson when the lights go down at the theater.

definition: Small bumps on the skin from cold, fear, or excitement.
etymology: A 19th-century coinage; the bumps were thought to resemble those on a plucked goose.
exampleSentence: I get goosebumps every time I hear that recording.

definition: A momentary trembling movement, especially from cold or thrill.
etymology: From Middle English 'chiveren,' of uncertain origin.
exampleSentence: A small shiver ran through me when I read his last sentence.

definition: An involuntary shaking movement; a small earthquake.
etymology: From Latin 'tremor,' meaning shaking, from 'tremere' (to tremble).
exampleSentence: There was a tiny tremor in his voice during the toast.

definition: An abrupt rough movement; a sudden shock.
etymology: Recorded in the late 16th century, perhaps from earlier 'jot,' a variant of 'jut.'
exampleSentence: The news was a jolt — none of us saw it coming.

definition: A violent or sudden change or disruption.
etymology: Formed in the 19th century from 'up' and 'heave,' originally of Germanic origin.
exampleSentence: The move was a small upheaval but worth it.

definition: Continuous change.
etymology: From Latin 'fluxus,' meaning flow, from 'fluere' (to flow).
exampleSentence: His schedule is in flux until the project ships.

definition: Lasting only for a short time; impermanent.
etymology: From Latin 'transiens,' present participle of 'transire' (to cross over).
exampleSentence: The good light at sunset is transient — you have about ten minutes.

definition: Not permanent; passing.
etymology: From late Latin 'transitorius,' from 'transire' (to pass over).
exampleSentence: Most arguments turn out to be transitory if you wait a day.

definition: Lasting for a very short time.
etymology: From Old English 'fleotan,' to float or swim, of Germanic origin.
exampleSentence: There was a fleeting look on his face I couldn't read.

definition: Lasting for a very short period.
etymology: From late Latin 'momentarius,' from 'momentum' (a moment).
exampleSentence: A momentary hesitation, and then he stepped on stage.

definition: Never ending or changing.
etymology: From Latin 'perpetualis,' from 'perpetuus' (continuous).
exampleSentence: There's a perpetual pile of mail on the kitchen counter.

definition: Lasting through many years; recurring constantly.
etymology: From Latin 'perennis,' from 'per-' (through) and 'annus' (year).
exampleSentence: Parking is a perennial complaint at every council meeting.

definition: Enduring; lasting a long time.
etymology: Present participle of 'abide,' from Old English 'abidan,' from 'a-' (and) 'bidan' (to wait).
exampleSentence: She has an abiding love for terrible action movies.

definition: Resolutely or dutifully firm and unwavering.
etymology: From Old English 'stedefaest,' from 'stede' (place) and 'faest' (firm).
exampleSentence: He's a steadfast friend in the actual sense of the word.

definition: Loyal, reliable, and hardworking.
etymology: From Old English 'stalworth,' meaning serviceable, of Germanic origin.
exampleSentence: The library has a few stalwart volunteers who keep the place running.

definition: Steady or resolute; not weakening.
etymology: Formed from 'un-' and 'waver,' from Middle English 'waveren,' to fluctuate.
exampleSentence: His unwavering optimism is occasionally annoying.

definition: Admirably purposeful, determined, and unwavering.
etymology: From Latin 'resolutus,' past participle of 'resolvere' (to loosen or settle).
exampleSentence: She was resolute about quitting refined sugar — for nine days.

definition: Refusing to be persuaded or to change one's mind.
etymology: From Greek 'adamas,' meaning unbreakable, from 'a-' (not) and 'daman' (to subdue).
exampleSentence: He was adamant that we not split the bill.

definition: Stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion.
etymology: From Latin 'obstinatus,' past participle of 'obstinare' (to persist).
exampleSentence: My grandmother is gloriously obstinate about her recipes.

definition: The quality of holding on firmly; persistence.
etymology: From Latin 'tenacitas,' from 'tenax' (holding fast).
exampleSentence: He runs his small business on coffee and pure tenacity.

definition: Persistence in doing something despite difficulty.
etymology: From Latin 'perseverantia,' from 'perseverare' (to persist).
exampleSentence: Sourdough is mostly a perseverance hobby.

definition: Firm or obstinate continuance in a course of action.
etymology: From Latin 'persistere' (to continue steadily), from 'per-' and 'sistere' (to stand).
exampleSentence: It took persistence to track down the original recipe.

definition: Firm determination to do something.
etymology: From Latin 'resolvere,' meaning to loosen or settle, from 're-' and 'solvere.'
exampleSentence: My New Year's resolve usually lasts until February.

definition: Control exerted to do something or restrain impulses.
etymology: A 19th-century compound from 'will' (volition) and 'power.'
exampleSentence: It takes willpower to walk past the bakery without going in.

definition: The force that makes something happen or happen more quickly.
etymology: From Latin 'impetus,' meaning an assault, from 'impetere' (to attack).
exampleSentence: The funding gave us the impetus to actually start.

definition: The impetus and driving force of a moving object or process.
etymology: From Latin 'momentum,' a contraction of 'movimentum,' from 'movere' (to move).
exampleSentence: The team had momentum heading into the playoffs.

definition: A person or thing that precipitates an event.
etymology: From Greek 'katalyein,' to dissolve, from 'kata-' (down) and 'lyein' (to loosen).
exampleSentence: That essay was the catalyst for changing careers.

definition: A situation in which no progress is possible.
etymology: From French 'impasse,' meaning a blind alley, from 'in-' (not) and 'passer' (to pass).
exampleSentence: The negotiations hit an impasse over remote work.

definition: A state of perplexity or uncertainty.
etymology: Recorded in the 16th century, of obscure origin, possibly a corruption of Latin 'quando' (when).
exampleSentence: I'm in a quandary about whether to tell her or not.

definition: A confusing and difficult problem.
etymology: Recorded in the late 16th century as university slang, of unknown origin.
exampleSentence: How to seat the in-laws is the holiday conundrum.

definition: A difficult or unpleasant situation.
etymology: From late Latin 'praedicamentum,' originally meaning 'category' in logic.
exampleSentence: He found himself in a predicament with two dates on the same night.

definition: A dangerous or difficult situation.
etymology: From Old English 'pliht,' meaning danger or peril, of Germanic origin.
exampleSentence: The plight of the local bookstore moved the whole town to help.

definition: A complicated or confused situation.
etymology: From Dutch 'moeras,' meaning marsh, from Old French 'maresc,' of Germanic origin.
exampleSentence: The paperwork was a morass none of us wanted to enter.

definition: A difficult, precarious, or entrapping situation.
etymology: From obsolete 'quag' (marsh) plus 'mire,' both of Germanic origin.
exampleSentence: Group chats can be a real quagmire.

definition: A complicated, irregular network of passages; a maze.
etymology: From Greek 'labyrinthos,' the mythical maze on Crete that housed the Minotaur.
exampleSentence: The hospital is a labyrinth and the signs are useless.

definition: A network of paths designed as a puzzle.
etymology: From Old English 'amasian' (to bewilder), of obscure origin.
exampleSentence: That old neighborhood is a maze if you don't have GPS.

definition: A network of interconnecting rabbit burrows; a densely populated area.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman 'warenne,' meaning a game preserve, of Germanic origin.
exampleSentence: The old market is a warren of stalls and side passages.

definition: To follow a winding course; to wander aimlessly.
etymology: From the Maeander, a famously winding river in modern-day Turkey.
exampleSentence: We meandered through the market for hours.

definition: To walk at an easy, leisurely pace.
etymology: From Old French 'ambler,' from Latin 'ambulare' (to walk).
exampleSentence: They ambled toward the lake, in no rush at all.

definition: To walk or travel through a place.
etymology: From Latin 'perambulare,' from 'per-' (through) and 'ambulare' (to walk).
exampleSentence: He likes to perambulate the neighborhood at sunset.

definition: To walk or move wearily or reluctantly.
etymology: Origin obscure; recorded in the 16th century.
exampleSentence: We traipsed across town only to find the place closed.

definition: To walk slowly and with heavy steps.
etymology: Recorded in the late 16th century, of obscure origin.
exampleSentence: He trudged home through the snow, balancing his groceries.

definition: To walk doggedly and slowly with heavy steps.
etymology: Recorded in the late 16th century, probably imitative of the sound.
exampleSentence: We plodded up the last hill, mostly out of stubbornness.

definition: A long, arduous journey.
etymology: From Afrikaans 'trek' (to pull), from Dutch 'trekken,' originally describing the long ox-cart journeys of Boer settlers.
exampleSentence: The trek to my favorite ramen place is exactly thirty minutes.

definition: A long and eventful journey.
etymology: From Greek 'Odysseia,' the title of Homer's epic poem about Odysseus's ten-year journey home.
exampleSentence: My quest for the right rain jacket has been an odyssey.

definition: A journey to a place regarded as having special significance.
etymology: From Old French 'pelegrinage,' from Latin 'peregrinus' (foreign).
exampleSentence: Every fall they make a pilgrimage to that cider mill.

definition: A long journey, especially by sea or in space.
etymology: From Old French 'veiage,' from Latin 'viaticum' (provisions for a journey).
exampleSentence: Their voyage to the islands was the trip of a lifetime.

definition: A journey undertaken with a particular purpose.
etymology: From Latin 'expeditio,' from 'expedire' (to free, prepare), from 'ex-' and 'pes' (foot).
exampleSentence: A trip to the grocery store with a toddler is its own expedition.

definition: A brief attempt or venture into something new.
etymology: From Old French 'forrer,' meaning to forage, of Germanic origin.
exampleSentence: His first foray into baking yielded one excellent biscuit and a smoke alarm.

definition: To accept or act in accordance with; to dwell.
etymology: From Old English 'abidan,' from 'a-' (intensifier) and 'bidan' (to wait).
exampleSentence: They abided in that cabin for two weeks with no plans.

definition: Traveling from place to place.
etymology: From Late Latin 'itinerans,' from 'itinerari' (to travel), from 'iter' (journey).
exampleSentence: He had an itinerant year doing odd jobs across the West.

definition: Living the life of a nomad; wandering.
etymology: From Greek 'nomadikos,' from 'nomas' (wandering).
exampleSentence: Her thirties were a nomadic decade, mostly by choice.

definition: A person who wanders from place to place without a home.
etymology: From Latin 'vagabundus,' from 'vagari' (to wander).
exampleSentence: He spent a vagabond summer with a guitar and a friend's couch.

definition: A person who stays in a place temporarily.
etymology: From the verb 'sojourn,' from Old French 'sojorner.'
exampleSentence: She felt like a sojourner in her own neighborhood after the long trip.

definition: A person who leaves their own country to settle in another.
etymology: From Latin 'emigrans,' present participle of 'emigrare,' from 'e-' (out) and 'migrare' (to move).
exampleSentence: My great-grandmother was an emigrant who never went back.

definition: The dispersion of a people from their original homeland.
etymology: From Greek 'diaspora,' meaning dispersion, from 'dia-' (across) and 'speirein' (to scatter).
exampleSentence: The food scene has been shaped by the city's many diasporas.

definition: The state of being barred from one's home, especially for political reasons.
etymology: From Latin 'exilium,' from 'exul' (banished person).
exampleSentence: He spent a decade in self-imposed exile from his hometown.

definition: To send someone away from a place as official punishment.
etymology: From Old French 'baniss-,' stem of 'banir,' of Germanic origin.
exampleSentence: My grandfather banished the cat from the kitchen for years.

definition: To absolve from blame or wrongdoing.
etymology: From Latin 'exoneratus,' past participle of 'exonerare' (to unburden).
exampleSentence: The new evidence completely exonerated her.

definition: To declare free from guilt or obligation.
etymology: From Latin 'absolvere,' from 'ab-' (from) and 'solvere' (to loosen).
exampleSentence: He absolved me of the dinner I'd forgotten to cook.

definition: To clear of blame; to show to be justified.
etymology: From Latin 'vindicare,' meaning to claim or avenge, from 'vindex' (claimant).
exampleSentence: The test results vindicated her hunch about the dough.

definition: To show that someone is not guilty of wrongdoing.
etymology: From medieval Latin 'exculpatus,' from 'ex-' (out) and 'culpa' (blame).
exampleSentence: His alibi was solid enough to exculpate him.

definition: Deserving blame.
etymology: From Latin 'culpabilis,' from 'culpa' (fault).
exampleSentence: We were all a little culpable for the late departure.

definition: Involved with others in an illegal or wrongful activity.
etymology: A back-formation from 'complicity,' from French 'complicité,' from Latin 'complicare' (to fold together).
exampleSentence: The dog stared at the chewed shoe, fully complicit.

definition: Fault; guilt — especially in the phrase 'mea culpa.'
etymology: From Latin 'culpa,' meaning fault, used in the Catholic Confiteor.
exampleSentence: Mea culpa — I forgot to plug in the slow cooker.

definition: Sincere remorse for wrongdoing.
etymology: From Latin 'contritio,' from 'contritus,' past participle of 'conterere' (to grind together).
exampleSentence: His contrition seemed real this time.

definition: Deep regret for a wrong committed.
etymology: From Latin 'remorsus,' past participle of 'remordere' (to bite back).
exampleSentence: There was no remorse for the missing piece of cake, just frosting on her chin.

definition: A feeling of guilt that prevents one from acting.
etymology: From Latin 'compunctio,' from 'compungere' (to prick sharply).
exampleSentence: He had no compunction about parking in the bike lane.

definition: A moral hesitation about a course of action.
etymology: From Latin 'scrupulus,' a small sharp stone, figuratively a worry.
exampleSentence: She has scruples about working for an oil company.

definition: A feeling of doubt or unease about one's conduct.
etymology: Possibly from Old English 'cwealm' (death), or related to Dutch 'kwalm' (vapor).
exampleSentence: He had no qualms about ordering the most expensive thing on the menu.

definition: A feeling of doubt or apprehension.
etymology: Formed in the 16th century from 'mis-' and 'give' in the sense of 'cause to be uneasy.'
exampleSentence: I had misgivings about the dress code, but it turned out fine.

definition: A feeling of fear or anxiety about something that may happen.
etymology: From Latin 'trepidatio,' from 'trepidare' (to be agitated), from 'trepidus' (alarmed).
exampleSentence: She approached the audition with real trepidation.

definition: A feeling that something bad will happen.
etymology: From the verb 'forebode,' from Old English 'forebodian' (to predict).
exampleSentence: There was a vague foreboding all afternoon, even before the news.

definition: A strong feeling that something is about to happen.
etymology: From late Latin 'praemonitio,' from 'praemonere' (to warn beforehand).
exampleSentence: I had a small premonition I should check on my plants.

definition: An intuitive feeling about the future, especially of misfortune.
etymology: From French 'pressentiment,' from 'pressentir' (to sense beforehand).
exampleSentence: He had a presentiment about the flight that he ignored, fortunately.

definition: A slight knowledge or suspicion; a hint.
etymology: From Middle English 'ningkiling,' meaning a whisper or undertone, of obscure origin.
exampleSentence: I didn't have the faintest inkling she'd been promoted.

definition: The ability to understand something instinctively.
etymology: From late Latin 'intuitio,' from 'intueri' (to look upon).
exampleSentence: Her intuition about the new hire turned out to be right.

definition: A feeling or guess based on intuition.
etymology: From the verb 'hunch' (to push or shove), the figurative sense developing in 19th-century American English.
exampleSentence: I had a hunch the chef was going to leave.

definition: Instinctive feeling rather than rational thinking.
etymology: From Old English 'guttas' (entrails), the figurative sense developing in the 20th century.
exampleSentence: My gut said no, and my gut was right.

definition: An innate, typically fixed pattern of behavior; a natural intuition.
etymology: From Latin 'instinctus,' from 'instinguere' (to incite).
exampleSentence: Her first instinct was to call her mother.

definition: Sharpness or keenness of thought, vision, or hearing.
etymology: From Latin 'acuitas,' from 'acuere' (to sharpen).
exampleSentence: Her mental acuity at 92 is genuinely intimidating.

definition: Clarity or lucidity of expression.
etymology: From Latin 'perspicuitas,' from 'perspicere' (to see through).
exampleSentence: His writing has a rare perspicuity that even non-experts can follow.

definition: Excessively lengthy or technical speech or writing.
etymology: From French 'verbiage,' from 'verbier' (to chatter), from 'verbe' (word).
exampleSentence: Cut the verbiage and tell me what you actually want.

definition: Using or containing too many words; tediously lengthy.
etymology: From Latin 'prolixus,' meaning extended, from 'pro-' (forward) and 'liqui' (to flow).
exampleSentence: His emails are prolix, but if you read them, they're actually thoughtful.

definition: Not or no longer needed; repetitive.
etymology: From Latin 'redundans,' present participle of 'redundare' (to overflow).
exampleSentence: Three redundant safety features kept the brakes from failing.

definition: Unnecessary, especially through being more than enough.
etymology: From Latin 'superfluus,' from 'super-' (over) and 'fluere' (to flow).
exampleSentence: Most of his furniture was superfluous and he sold half of it.

definition: Irrelevant or unrelated to the subject being dealt with.
etymology: From Latin 'extraneus,' meaning external, from 'extra' (outside).
exampleSentence: Cut the extraneous detail and the recipe is actually simple.

definition: Relevant or applicable to a particular matter.
etymology: From Latin 'pertinens,' present participle of 'pertinere' (to belong to).
exampleSentence: She had one pertinent observation that changed the meeting.

definition: Closely connected to the matter in hand.
etymology: From medieval Latin 'relevans,' from 'relevare' (to raise up).
exampleSentence: None of his stories are technically relevant, but they're great.

definition: Diverging from a previous course; only slightly relevant.
etymology: From Latin 'tangens' (touching), from 'tangere' (to touch).
exampleSentence: He has a habit of going off on tangential rants about parking.

definition: Neither parallel nor at a right angle; indirect.
etymology: From Latin 'obliquus,' meaning slanting.
exampleSentence: She made an oblique reference to the layoffs.

definition: Longer than the most direct route.
etymology: From medieval Latin 'circuitosus,' from 'circuitus' (a going around).
exampleSentence: He took a circuitous route home, through the riverside park.

definition: Extremely complex and difficult to follow.
etymology: From Latin 'convolutus,' past participle of 'convolvere' (to roll together).
exampleSentence: The plot was so convoluted I had to look up a summary.

definition: Like a labyrinth; complicated.
etymology: From 'labyrinth,' from Greek 'labyrinthos.'
exampleSentence: The application process was labyrinthine, but she got the visa.

definition: Excessively complicated, typically involving a great deal of intrigue.
etymology: From the Byzantine Empire, whose government was famed in the West for its complexity and intrigue.
exampleSentence: The seating chart for the wedding became byzantine.

definition: Having an untidy appearance.
etymology: From 'un-' and obsolete 'kempt' (combed), from Old English 'cemban' (to comb).
exampleSentence: He has a deliberately unkempt look that takes thirty minutes.

definition: In a state of disarray; untidy.
etymology: From Old French 'descheveler,' from 'des-' (un-) and 'chevel' (hair).
exampleSentence: He arrived disheveled but glowing, fresh off a red-eye.

definition: Untidy and dirty.
etymology: Recorded in the 16th century from 'sloven' (a careless person), of obscure origin.
exampleSentence: His apartment had a charming, almost slovenly quality.

definition: Done with great care and thoroughness.
etymology: Formed in the 16th century from 'pains' (effort) and 'taking,' suggesting effort given to a task.
exampleSentence: He's painstaking about his fishing flies.

definition: In accordance with the highest standards; faultless.
etymology: From Latin 'impeccabilis,' from 'in-' (not) and 'peccare' (to sin).
exampleSentence: Her timing in stand-up is impeccable.

definition: Without any imperfections.
etymology: Formed from 'flaw' (from Old Norse 'flaga,' a flake) and the suffix '-less.'
exampleSentence: The wedding was flawless, except for the speech, which was incredible.

definition: Not changed or impaired; kept in its original natural state.
etymology: Formed from 'un-' and 'spoil,' from Old French 'espoillier,' from Latin 'spoliare' (to strip).
exampleSentence: The beach was unspoiled on the morning we arrived.

definition: No longer existing or functioning.
etymology: From Latin 'defunctus,' past participle of 'defungi' (to finish, to complete).
exampleSentence: The defunct factory has been turned into apartments.

definition: No longer produced or used; out of date.
etymology: From Latin 'obsoletus,' past participle of 'obsolescere' (to fall into disuse).
exampleSentence: My printer drivers are obsolete, of course.

definition: Very old or old-fashioned.
etymology: From Greek 'arkhaikos,' from 'arkhaios' (ancient), from 'arkhe' (beginning).
exampleSentence: The dress code is archaic but the food is excellent.

definition: Old-fashioned or outdated.
etymology: From Latin 'antiquatus,' past participle of 'antiquare' (to make old).
exampleSentence: My office still uses antiquated phones with cords.

definition: Attractively unusual or old-fashioned.
etymology: From Old French 'cointe,' meaning skillful or clever, from Latin 'cognitus' (known).
exampleSentence: The shop is quaint without trying too hard.

definition: Pleasant or attractive.
etymology: From Old French 'charme,' meaning enchantment, from Latin 'carmen' (song or incantation).
exampleSentence: It's a charming neighborhood with one of every kind of store.

definition: Inspiring affection.
etymology: From the verb 'endear,' formed in the 17th century from 'en-' and 'dear.'
exampleSentence: His habit of singing while he cooks is genuinely endearing.

definition: Attractive or appealing in a fresh, innocent way.
etymology: From Old English 'wynsum,' meaning pleasant, from 'wynn' (joy).
exampleSentence: She has a winsome way of agreeing with you that makes you want to be right.

definition: Charming and attractive.
etymology: Present participle of 'engage,' from Old French 'engagier' (to pledge).
exampleSentence: He's an engaging speaker even on dry topics.

definition: Capable of attracting and holding interest; charming.
etymology: Present participle of 'captivate,' from late Latin 'captivare' (to take captive).
exampleSentence: Her voice on the album is captivating from the first track.

definition: Completely engrossing; compelling.
etymology: From 'rivet,' a metal pin, suggesting being fastened in place.
exampleSentence: The documentary was somehow riveting despite being about office chairs.

definition: Capturing fascinated attention.
etymology: From 'enthrall,' originally meaning to enslave, from 'thrall' (a slave).
exampleSentence: The musician's set was completely enthralling.

definition: To capture the complete attention of.
etymology: After Franz Mesmer, an 18th-century physician who believed in 'animal magnetism.'
exampleSentence: The little glass blower's torch absolutely mesmerized the kids.

definition: Capable of producing a state of fascinated attention.
etymology: From Greek 'hypnotikos,' from 'hypnos' (sleep).
exampleSentence: The rhythm of the train tracks is hypnotic.

definition: A half-conscious state characterized by an absence of response to external stimuli.
etymology: From Old French 'transe,' meaning a passage from life to death, from Latin 'transire' (to cross).
exampleSentence: I fell into a trance scrolling through old photos.

definition: A state of deep, melancholy thought.
etymology: Recorded in the 16th century; 'brown' here meant gloomy or serious, and 'study' meant a state of pondering.
exampleSentence: He'd drift into a brown-study about his hometown after a glass of wine.

definition: A pleasant sequence of thoughts diverting the mind from work.
etymology: A 17th-century compound of 'day' and 'dream.'
exampleSentence: My most productive thinking happens during daydreams.

definition: Indulgence in aimless thought or dreamy imagining.
etymology: From the actual practice of gathering tufts of wool caught on bushes, a slow, inattentive task.
exampleSentence: Sorry — I was woolgathering, can you repeat the question?

definition: A period of reflection or thought.
etymology: From Old French 'muser,' meaning to ponder, possibly from 'mus' (snout), suggesting nose-in-the-air pondering.
exampleSentence: The book is mostly musings, but very good ones.

definition: The act of thinking carefully about something.
etymology: From 'ponder,' from Latin 'ponderare' (to weigh).
exampleSentence: After much pondering, he ordered the cheeseburger.

definition: The action of looking thoughtfully at something for a long time.
etymology: From Latin 'contemplatio,' from 'contemplari' (to gaze attentively at).
exampleSentence: He spent the morning in contemplation of the bird feeder.

definition: The action of thinking deeply or focusing the mind.
etymology: From Latin 'meditatio,' from 'meditari' (to think over).
exampleSentence: Twenty minutes of meditation is hard, but worth it.

definition: The examination of one's own thoughts and feelings.
etymology: From Latin 'introspicere' (to look within), from 'intro-' and 'specere' (to look).
exampleSentence: A long flight is good for introspection, whether you want it or not.

definition: Serious thought or consideration.
etymology: From Latin 'reflexio,' from 'reflectere' (to bend back).
exampleSentence: On reflection, the move turned out to be the right call.

definition: Survey or review of a past course of events.
etymology: From Latin 'retrospectus,' past participle of 'retrospicere' (to look back).
exampleSentence: In retrospect, leaving the umbrella at home was optimistic.

definition: Understanding of a situation only after it has happened.
etymology: A 19th-century compound of 'hind' (rear) and 'sight.'
exampleSentence: Hindsight is unhelpful but very comforting.

definition: The ability to predict or prepare for the future.
etymology: From Old English 'foreseon' (to see beforehand), from 'fore-' and 'seon' (to see).
exampleSentence: It took some foresight to plant the bulbs in October.

definition: The fact of knowing something before it takes place.
etymology: From Latin 'praescientia,' from 'praescire' (to know beforehand).
exampleSentence: His prescience about the housing market was either skill or luck.

definition: Having the supposed power to see things beyond normal perception.
etymology: From French 'clairvoyant,' literally 'clear-seeing,' from 'clair' (clear) and 'voyant' (seeing).
exampleSentence: It felt almost clairvoyant when she texted me right then.

definition: Accurately predicting what will happen.
etymology: From Greek 'prophetikos,' from 'prophetes' (one who speaks beforehand).
exampleSentence: His warning about the storm turned out to be prophetic.

definition: Like an oracle; mysteriously profound.
etymology: From Latin 'oraculum,' meaning a divine pronouncement, from 'orare' (to speak).
exampleSentence: His advice is oracular — wise but you have to figure it out yourself.

definition: Difficult to interpret or understand; mysterious.
etymology: From Greek 'ainigma,' meaning a riddle, from 'ainissesthai' (to speak in riddles).
exampleSentence: She gave an enigmatic smile when I asked who she'd voted for.

definition: Having a meaning that is mysterious or obscure.
etymology: From Greek 'kryptikos,' from 'kryptos' (hidden).
exampleSentence: His texts are always cryptic but eventually make sense.

definition: Impossible to understand or interpret.
etymology: From late Latin 'inscrutabilis,' from 'in-' (not) and 'scrutari' (to search).
exampleSentence: My cat's mood is inscrutable on the best of days.

definition: Completely baffling.
etymology: From Latin 'perplexus,' meaning intricate, from 'per-' and 'plectere' (to plait).
exampleSentence: The instructions were perplexing but the cake came out fine.

definition: Impossible to understand; perplexing.
etymology: From 'baffle,' of uncertain origin but recorded in 16th-century Scots meaning to disgrace.
exampleSentence: It's baffling that nobody mentioned the time change.

definition: To bewilder or perplex someone.
etymology: Recorded in the 19th century, of uncertain origin, possibly imitative.
exampleSentence: That last clue completely flummoxed me.

definition: To puzzle or bewilder.
etymology: Coined in the 18th century from 'be-' and 'muse' in the sense of to ponder.
exampleSentence: He looked bemused but went along with the plan.

definition: To disconcert or confuse.
etymology: A fanciful 19th-century American coinage, likely a mock-Latin alteration of 'discompose.'
exampleSentence: The new layout of the grocery store completely discombobulated me.

definition: By some chance; perhaps.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman French 'par cheance' (by chance).
exampleSentence: Perchance there's a slice of pie left in the fridge.

definition: Truly; certainly.
etymology: From Middle English 'verraily,' from 'verray' (very, true), from Latin 'verax' (true).
exampleSentence: Verily, this is the best cup of coffee I've had this week.

definition: Indeed; in truth (often archaic or ironic).
etymology: From Old English 'forsoth,' from 'for' and 'soth' (truth).
exampleSentence: Forsooth, my keys were in my coat the whole time.

definition: From what place or source.
etymology: From Middle English 'whennes,' from Old English 'hwanon' (from where).
exampleSentence: I have no idea whence this houseplant came.

definition: To or toward this place.
etymology: From Old English 'hider,' related to 'her' (here).
exampleSentence: Come hither and look at this strange cloud.

definition: At some distance in the direction indicated.
etymology: From Middle English 'yond,' from Old English 'geond' (over there).
exampleSentence: The coffee shop is over yonder, past the library.

definition: In a quick and skillful way.
etymology: From 'deft,' from Old English 'gedaefte' (mild or gentle), which later took on the sense of skilled.
exampleSentence: She deftly defused the awkward question.

definition: Skillfully; with cleverness.
etymology: From French 'adroit,' literally 'to the right,' meaning correct or proper.
exampleSentence: He adroitly changed the subject before things got tense.

definition: Neatness and skill.
etymology: From 'deft,' from Old English 'gedaefte.'
exampleSentence: The waiter cleared the table with real deftness.

definition: Skill in performing tasks, especially with the hands.
etymology: From Latin 'dexteritas,' from 'dexter' (on the right side).
exampleSentence: The dexterity required to fold a fitted sheet is underrated.

definition: Able to move quickly and easily.
etymology: From Latin 'agilis,' from 'agere' (to do or drive).
exampleSentence: For seventy, he's remarkably agile on a ladder.

definition: Quick and light in movement or thought.
etymology: From Old English 'numol,' meaning capable of taking, related to 'niman' (to take).
exampleSentence: You have to be nimble in this market to keep up.

definition: Slim, supple, and graceful.
etymology: From Old English 'lithe,' meaning soft or mild, of Germanic origin.
exampleSentence: The dancers were lithe and exact.

definition: Bending and moving easily; flexible.
etymology: From Old French 'souple,' from Latin 'supplex' (submissive).
exampleSentence: The leather was supple, broken in by years.

definition: Having many curves and turns; lithe and flexible.
etymology: From Latin 'sinuosus,' from 'sinus' (a bend or curve).
exampleSentence: The road takes a sinuous path along the cliffs.

definition: Winding or curving like a snake.
etymology: From Latin 'serpentinus,' from 'serpens' (serpent).
exampleSentence: The line at the airport was serpentine, but moved quickly.

definition: Full of twists and turns.
etymology: From Latin 'tortuosus,' from 'torquere' (to twist).
exampleSentence: The path to the cabin is tortuous but beautiful in the fall.

definition: Extremely difficult or complicated.
etymology: From Old English 'cnotta' (a knot), the figurative sense developing in the 14th century.
exampleSentence: The plot was knotty but emotionally satisfying.

definition: Very complicated or detailed.
etymology: From Latin 'intricatus,' past participle of 'intricare' (to entangle).
exampleSentence: The cake had an intricate sugar design that wobbled when we cut it.

definition: Involving many carefully arranged parts.
etymology: From Latin 'elaboratus,' past participle of 'elaborare' (to work out).
exampleSentence: He made an elaborate breakfast that took two hours.

definition: Elaborately or highly decorated.
etymology: From Latin 'ornatus,' past participle of 'ornare' (to adorn).
exampleSentence: The mirror was too ornate for the simple hallway.

definition: Highly ornate and extravagant in style.
etymology: From Portuguese 'barroco,' meaning an irregular pearl, used to describe an artistic style.
exampleSentence: The dessert had a baroque presentation that didn't really help the flavor.

definition: Highly elaborate, especially in decoration.
etymology: From French 'rococo,' a fanciful alteration of 'rocaille' (rock work).
exampleSentence: The lobby has a rococo charm that's growing on me.

definition: Severe or strict; plain and unadorned.
etymology: From Greek 'austeros,' meaning harsh or rough.
exampleSentence: The chapel was austere but warm somehow.

definition: Showing self-discipline; austere.
etymology: From the ancient Greek city of Sparta, whose citizens were known for simple, disciplined living.
exampleSentence: His apartment is spartan — bed, chair, books, that's it.

definition: Characterized by severe self-discipline and abstention from pleasure.
etymology: From Greek 'asketikos,' from 'asketes' (one who exercises), originally of athletes.
exampleSentence: He led an ascetic life for one month every year, no coffee included.

definition: Not self-indulgent, especially regarding food and drink.
etymology: From Latin 'abstemius,' meaning sober, from 'abs-' and 'temetum' (strong drink).
exampleSentence: He's abstemious at lunch but generous with dessert.

definition: Moderation or self-restraint.
etymology: From Latin 'temperantia,' from 'temperare' (to mix or moderate).
exampleSentence: His temperance lasted three days into the holidays.

definition: The avoidance of excess.
etymology: From Latin 'moderatio,' from 'moderari' (to regulate).
exampleSentence: All things in moderation, including moderation itself.

definition: Self-control; a measure that limits.
etymology: From Old French 'restraindre,' from Latin 'restringere' (to bind back).
exampleSentence: He showed real restraint at the dessert table.

definition: Training to act in accordance with rules; controlled behavior.
etymology: From Latin 'disciplina,' from 'discipulus' (learner).
exampleSentence: It takes discipline to practice an hour every day, but she does.

definition: The action or state of keeping careful watch.
etymology: From Latin 'vigilantia,' from 'vigilare' (to keep awake).
exampleSentence: A little vigilance with the oven would have saved that loaf.

definition: The quality of being cautious or wise in practical matters.
etymology: From Latin 'prudentia,' a contraction of 'providentia' (foresight).
exampleSentence: It was pure prudence to bring an extra layer.

definition: Conformity to what is socially acceptable.
etymology: From Old French 'propriete,' from Latin 'proprietas' (property), from 'proprius' (one's own).
exampleSentence: She was raised on strict propriety and now finds it amusing.

definition: Behavior in keeping with good taste and propriety.
etymology: From Latin 'decorum,' neuter of 'decorus' (seemly).
exampleSentence: Even in a heated argument, he kept perfect decorum.

definition: The customary code of polite behavior.
etymology: From French 'etiquette,' originally meaning a small note (etiquette de la cour) outlining court ceremonies.
exampleSentence: Phone etiquette varies wildly by generation.

definition: The official procedure governing affairs of state or matters of conduct.
etymology: From Greek 'protokollon,' the first leaf glued to a manuscript with notes on its content, from 'protos' (first) and 'kolla' (glue).
exampleSentence: There's a whole protocol for greeting the bride.
